title: The Impact of Ending Mandatory Union Fees: Evidence from Administrative Data
affiliations: Villanova University - School of Business - Economics

detail.title: The Impact of Ending Mandatory Union Fees: Evidence from Administrative Data
detail.abstract: The 2018 Supreme Court decision in Janus v. AFSCME eliminated mandatory union fees for public-sector workers, overturning four decades of legal precedent. Using administrative payroll data from 400 jurisdictions across 21 states, I find that dues-paying membership declined by 8.9 to 13.4 percent by 2021, a drop substantially smaller than anticipated. At least three-quarters of this decline reflects the automatic termination of agency fees rather than voluntary exits by union members. Teachers, police, and firefighters maintained relatively stable membership, while support staff experienced declines of 13 to 18 percent. Despite these membership losses, I find no impact on overall earnings.

title: Ruled by Robots? Legal Feasibility of AI Agents in Corporate Management

detail.title: Ruled by Robots? Legal Feasibility of AI Agents in Corporate Management

detail.abstract: This article examines whether artificial intelligence may lawfully participate in corporate management under contemporary company law. Focusing on closely held companies, it argues that artificial intelligence may be deployed as a decision-support mechanism within corporate governance but cannot, under existing doctrine, assume the legal office or authority of a director or manager. That limit is not merely practical, it is structural. The law of corporate management remains anchored to natural persons capable of exercising judgement, bearing fiduciary and statutory duties, and being held to account for the exercise of corporate power. Through a comparative analysis of Australian and Brazilian law, and by reference to concrete governance workflows such as financial reporting, disclosure, and internal oversight, the article shows that current statutory frameworks continue to exclude the substitution of autonomous artificial intelligence for human decision-makers. Artificial intelligence is therefore best understood, at least for present purposes, as an instrument of governance rather than a legally cognisable corporate manager.

title: Consumer Behavior and Algorithmic Price Competition: The Case of Reference Dependence
affiliations: , University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Consumer Behavior and Algorithmic Price Competition: The Case of Reference Dependence
detail.abstract: As AI and humans increasingly coexist in the marketplace, it is important to understand how human psychology interacts with algorithmic decision-making. How do consumer behavioral patterns influence algorithmic pricing and the resulting profits and consumer welfare? Should consumer AI agents emulate human psychology or act rationally? While current wisdom suggests removing human biases to maximize efficiency, our paper investigates how consumers' reference dependence, a core human "bias", shapes market outcomes under algorithmic price competition. We show theoretically that reference dependence creates two opposing forces on equilibrium prices: higher demand elasticity disciplines prices downward, while easier collusion raises them. We resolve this tension using simulated experiments in which reinforcement-learning pricing algorithms compete repeatedly for reference-dependent consumers. We find that the disciplining effect dominates: reference dependence paradoxically acts as a competitive safeguard, driving prices down, consumer welfare up, and firm profits down, even as algorithms attempt to collude. These effects persist even when pricing algorithms do not account for behavioral demand features, when consumers are loss-averse, and under alternative assumptions on how consumers form reference prices. Human behavioral biases, while individually non-rational, can collectively discipline pricing and improve consumer outcomes, especially when facing algorithms. We discuss the implications of these findings for the design of consumer AI agents.

title: Commoditize Your Complement: Strategic Open-Source Releases and the Cannibalization of Rival Firms
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business

detail.title: Commoditize Your Complement: Strategic Open-Source Releases and the Cannibalization of Rival Firms
detail.abstract: Why do firms release open-source software for free? This paper investigates how dominant technology firms strategically release free open-source software (OSS) to commoditize complementary markets and devalue competitors' proprietary assets. Exploiting the staggered release of major GitHub repositories, I find that this strategy triggers a wealth transfer: focal firms experience a 13.9% increase in market valuation, capturing over $406 billion in aggregate wealth, while exposed rivals suffer a 7.6% decline. This strategy forces competitors into technological dependence, compelling them to shift human capital toward the focal firm's OSS. Consequently, while rivals experience a decline in sales, their forced adaptation yields cost efficiencies that inflate short-term profit margins. However, this defensive restructuring ultimately impairs their long-term innovation and product market dynamics: direct rivals decrease R&D expenditures by 14.8%, curtail exploratory innovation, and exhibit reduced product market fluidity. Ultimately, free OSS structurally reorganizes industry competition.

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract:
Gender diversity has emerged as a significant determinant of sustainability performance across global markets. Evidence from G20 economies indicates that firms prioritising gender diversity across organisational levels demonstrate stronger Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosure, enhanced market trust, and greater long-term resilience.

Against the backdrop of South Africa’s G20 presidency, which has sought to reposition the G20 toward developmental priorities and global equity, this paper examines the relationship between gender-balanced leadership and ESG performance. Focusing on Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE)-listed companies, the study draws on Risk Insights’ ESG GPS® dataset, covering over 340 ESG indicators across major African exchanges.

South Africa’s ESG ecosystem—anchored in King IV principles, JSE Listings Requirements, and sustainability disclosure guidance—provides a distinctive context for analysing how board composition influences ESG outcomes. As a member of the United Nations-supported Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative, the JSE has demonstrated leadership in promoting transparency and gender diversity, although disclosure depth remains uneven.

The findings show that companies with gender-balanced boards achieve higher ESG ratings and outperform peers, reinforcing gender diversity as both an ethical imperative and a measurable driver of competitiveness. The paper further integrates insights from G20 engagement groups (B20, C20, T20, W20, and G20 Empower) and proposes actionable pathways for embedding gender metrics into ESG frameworks, strengthening data comparability, and linking inclusive governance to sustainable finance.

title: Improving The Credibility Of Corporate Sustainability Metrics
affiliations: , University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Anderson School of Management (UCLA) and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Improving The Credibility Of Corporate Sustainability Metrics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding for this work

detail.abstract: Firms face growing pressure to measure and disclose their sustainability performance, yet credible sustainability metrics remain scarce because sustainability initiatives often operate under significant uncertainty. We argue that two forms of uncertainty—effect uncertainty (whether an initiative produces its intended outcome) and measurement uncertainty (the accuracy and stability of quantification)—fundamentally shape the credibility of sustainability metrics. We introduce a credibility-centered roadmap that helps managers diagnose these uncertainties, select metrics that fit the informational context, reduce uncertainty where feasible, communicate remaining uncertainty transparently, and pause quantitative disclosure when precision cannot be responsibly claimed. The roadmap recognizes that credibility depends on aligning disclosure with what can be responsibly known rather than choosing the "right" metric in the abstract. Using carbon offsets as an illustrative domain where both uncertainties are exceptionally high, we demonstrate how misaligned metrics can unintentionally mislead stakeholders and why process metrics, qualified outcomes, or strategic silence may be more credible than precise quantitative claims. By adopting this structured approach, organizations can design sustainability metrics that more accurately reflect what can be known, avoid overstating confidence, and strengthen stakeholder trust.

detail.title: Losers with Passports: Travel as a Mask for Emptiness in Literature and Late Modern Life

detail.abstract: This paper examines contemporary travel not as a practice of encounter or formation, but as a compensatory social ritual through which intellectual and moral emptiness is masked by movement. Drawing on the travel writing of Simone de Beauvoir, John Steinbeck, and the historical reflections of Tony Judt, the analysis reconstructs travel as a demanding practice historically tied to attention, restraint, and the capacity for return. The paper contrasts this tradition with late modern forms of demonstrative mobility, in which travel functions primarily as a spectacle of visibility and a substitute for internal formation. By tracing the erosion of risk, memory, and transformation in contemporary mobility, the study shows how travel increasingly produces repetition rather than change, exposure without encounter, and movement without meaning.

title: Physics-Based Analysis of Submarine Surface Signatures: Hydrodynamic Mechanisms, Detection Theory, and Countermeasure Constraints

detail.title: Physics-Based Analysis of Submarine Surface Signatures: Hydrodynamic Mechanisms, Detection Theory, and Countermeasure Constraints

detail.abstract:
Submarine survivability depends on the difficulty of detection, yet non-acoustic anti-submarine warfare increasingly exploits surface expressions of submerged motion. This paper develops a physics-based framework linking submarine-induced hydrodynamic disturbances to observable modulation in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) normalized radar cross section (NRCS). We analyze key surface-signature mechanisms including near-field pressure effects, internal-wave–driven roughness modulation, and wake-adjacent surfactant dynamics and characterize how environmental conditions (wind speed, sea state, and stratification) constrain observability.

To translate physical observability into operational detectability, we frame detection under non-Gaussian (K-distributed) sea clutter using a Neyman–Pearson/CFAR perspective and explicitly define the assumptions required to interpret signal-to-clutter requirements. We further examine how modern AI-based processing particularly convolutional and transformer-based architectures applied to SAR feature extraction and anomaly detection modifies the effective detection problem by integrating spatial context, multi-look statistics, and cross-sensor cueing. Rather than assuming AI “sees” submarines directly, we analyze how machine learning systems alter false-alarm tradeoffs, clutter discrimination, and probabilistic cue generation under bounded physical constraints.

Finally, we assess countermeasure feasibility by bounding timing, power, motion, and deployment constraints for surface-deployed deception systems intended to degrade SAR-based cueing and automated detection. The results support a bounded “translucent ocean” conclusion: satellite SAR, augmented by AI-driven inference, functions as a probabilistic cueing system whose effectiveness remains strongly conditional on environment, processing assumptions, and adversary countermeasures. The views expressed are solely those of the author and do not represent the views of any government, organization, or institution.

title: Referral Program Design: Thresholds and Cold Starts
affiliations: University College London - UCL School of Management

detail.title: Referral Program Design: Thresholds and Cold Starts
detail.abstract: We study the optimal design of referral programs when customers strategically communicate with multiple friends, trading off referral rewards, concerns about their friends' welfare, and the social cost of making suboptimal recommendations. Threshold-based referral programs are cost-effective in improving referral conversions. However, when customers are highly concerned about making suboptimal recommendations, such programs suffer from a cold-start problem, where the conversion rate stagnates at the no-program baseline, remaining unresponsive to increased referral rewards. An increase in this concern can make the friends worse off in equilibrium, as the firm scales up rewards to overcome the cold-start problem. Linear referral programs are less cost-effective but more robust to the cold-start problem, providing more immediate feedback on the program's performance when the firm iteratively fine-tunes its referral program. Our analysis clarifies the appeal and challenges of nonlinear referral programs and helps explain the observed popularity of linear referral programs.

title: Getting Sick from Colleagues' Absences through Cumulative Workload: Evidence from Home Nursing
affiliations: IESEG School of Management, Centre for Economics and Corporate Sustainability (CEDON), KULeuven, IESEG School of Management, Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 - LEM - Lille Economie Management and Catholic University of Lille - IÉSEG School of Management, Lille Campus

detail.title: Getting Sick from Colleagues' Absences through Cumulative Workload: Evidence from Home Nursing
detail.abstract: Sickness absence is widespread and costly, yet organizations rarely account for the full chain of consequences it sets in motion. When an employee is absent, their colleagues absorb the redistributed work. If that workload accumulates faster than workers can recover, it may compromise their own health and generate further absences. We study this relationship using monthly administrative data from 843 nurses in the largest home nursing organization in Flanders, Belgium, observed over twelve months. We construct a measure of cumulative workload using an exponential decay function over the prior three months and identify its causal effect on sickness absence through a two-stage least squares strategy that instruments individual cumulative workload with plausibly exogenous variation in regional colleague absence patterns. A one-standard-deviation increase in colleagues’ sickness absence and colleagues’ paid hours off over the previous three months increases the cumulative workload of remaining nurses through workload redistribution, which in turn raises a focal nurse’s monthly sick days by 0.47 days and the share of working time spent on sick leave by 2.13 percentage points. These findings are robust to alternative workload measures and decay parameters. We reveal an indirect cost channel of absenteeism that organizations do not currently measure. Each sick day generates approximately 0.14 additional sick days among colleagues in the following month through workload redistribution, representing a spillover cost of 26 euros per initial sick day. Workload-aware assignment policies could limit both the health burden on remaining workers and these hidden organizational costs.

detail.title: Energy Sufficiency as a New Model of Economic Development for the European Union

publicationDetails.detailsText: to be published in: World Development, 2026, Volume 5, Moscow: IMEMO (Russian Academy of Sciences)

detail.abstract: We have analyzed the concept of energy sufficiency as a logical continuation of Georgescu-Roegen's ecological economics of the 1970s and the basis of the European Union's current green course. The possibilities for implementing this development model in the next 5–7 years have been assessed. The author combined three political-economic approaches — A. Krueger's rent-seeking theory, P. Haas's theory of epistemic communities, and S. Strange's concept of “structural power” — for a comprehensive study of the normative and institutional mechanisms of the EU's energy transition. The empirical basis includes statistics on the industrial decline in the European Union in 2023–2024, data on European Central Bank investments, and data on meetings between lobbyists and European Commission officials. It has been found that the forced implementation of the sufficiency model accelerates deindustrialization and inflation and increases development imbalances between different regions of Europe. In addition, the expansion of lobbying networks contributes to the concentration of rentier income in the oil and gas sector and creates a symbiosis between the expert community and European Union institutions. The presentation clarifies the role of the energy sufficiency model in the context of the European Union's climate goals for 2030 and analyzes the unevenness of climate investment in the countries of North-Western and Central-Eastern Europe. It concludes that if the current trajectory of energy sufficiency is maintained, the freedom of economic actors will be limited and the European Union's dependence on external structural factors will increase. The article provides justification for refining the model's targets, harmonizing energy policy at the national level, and developing new cross-sectoral incentives for economic development.

title: When a Large Employer Comes to Town: Labor Market Entry and Corporate Disclosure
affiliations: McGill University - Desautels Faculty of Management

detail.title: When a Large Employer Comes to Town: Labor Market Entry and Corporate Disclosure
detail.abstract: This paper examines how incumbent firms adjust their disclosure behavior in response to heightened labor market competition. Using announcements of large employer entries into local labor markets, I find that incumbent firms located in the affected counties increase the disclosure of positive, forward-looking information. This response is concentrated among incumbent firms that compete more directly with entrant firms for similar workers and is strongest in local labor markets where employee retention pressures are likely to be more severe. Additional analyses show that the response extends to qualitative disclosure, particularly job-related and reputation-enhancing press releases, is associated with more favorable subsequent employment outcomes, and is unlikely to be explained by alternative motives related to productivity spillovers, supply-chain linkages, product market competition, or capital market considerations. Overall, the evidence supports the view that firms use public disclosure to shape employee perceptions and mitigate turnover risk when competition for talent intensifies.

title: How Technology Is Redefining the Role of the Modern Travel Consultant

detail.title: How Technology Is Redefining the Role of the Modern Travel Consultant
detail.abstract:
Travel is no longer just about getting from point A to point B. It’s about experiences, storytelling, memories that linger long after the plane lands, and moments that feel crafted just for you. For decades, travel consultants were the architects of these journeys. They memorized flight schedules, navigated visa labyrinths, maintained hotel and tour operator networks, and provided reassurance that every detail was accounted for. Their work was a blend of precision, knowledge, and intuition¹. But the world is changing. Travelers today wield more information than ever at their fingertips. Flight comparison websites, AI powered itinerary suggestions, online reviews, and virtual reality previews have made self-service planning increasingly accessible. In this environment, the travel consultant’s role is being reshaped—not eliminated. The modern travel consultant is evolving into a curator of experiences, a translator of data, and a guide through an increasingly complex travel ecosystem.
This transformation raises a fundamental question: in an age of apps, automation, and online booking engines, what unique value does a human travel consultant bring? The answer lies not just in expertise, but in creativity, empathy, and the ability to weave technology into experiences that feel personal, seamless, and unforgettable.

detail.abstract: I study how firms’ defensive investments affect aggregate total factor productivity in a general-equilibrium model where incumbents invest both to raise productivity and to deter entry or imitation; entry occurs either by new firms into existing markets or by leading firms in entirely new product lines. Calibrating the model to US firm size, productivity, and market share distributions, I find that cracking down on defensive investments increases TFP by 1.9 percent, about three-quarters of which reflects higher technical efficiency, driven mainly by improved firm-level productivity. This gain is substantially offset by reduced product variety; absent this loss, the TFP effect would be more than four times as large. Profit taxes targeted at high-productivity leaders – those most prone to block imitation – can stimulate frontier innovation while limiting variety losses. Firm-level US evidence supports these mechanisms.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Charles University in Prague Faculty of Law Research Paper No. 2026/I/1
publicationDetails.journalName: Charles University in Prague Faculty of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article examines literary freedom in France and Czechoslovakia during the détente period (1962-1974), demonstrating significant parallels despite different political systems. Through chronological and thematic analyses, it reveals that both countries experienced similar trajectories: initial liberalization (1962-1968) culminating in the transformative year 1968, followed by repressive measures. The study challenges binary interpretations of May-June 68 and the Prague Spring, showing both simultaneity and similarity in their evolution of literary freedom. Key commonalities emerge across both contexts: writers' influence on free speech legislation, post-1968 repression, transformation of censorial institutions from traditional preventive censorship toward economic control mechanisms, increasing tolerance for genre literature (science fiction, detective fiction), and the impact of sexual liberation on literary production. The year 1968 serves as a pivotal moment, marking both the apex of liberalization and the beginning of institutional backlash temporary in France under Giscard d'Estaing, prolonged in Czechoslovakia under Husák's normalization. However, the comparison also reveals nationally-specific repressions, particularly France's censorship of anticolonial and anti-imperialist writings. The article proceeds through two complementary approaches: first, a chronological analysis identifying 1968 as a watershed moment; second, a thematic examination of tensions between political discourse and aesthetic writing, confirming the hypothesis of meaningful similarity between French and Czechoslovak experiences of literary freedom during détente.

detail.title: Reconceptualizing Judicial Activism: Intervention Versus Involvement in the Israeli Supreme Court

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Law and Empirical Analysis 2024, Vol. 1(2) 343–357

detail.abstract: The paper conceptualizes two distinct yet interconnected modes of judicial activism: courts as intervening in the policies and actions of other branches of government and courts as involved in their policymaking process. It proposes empirical methods to assess these modes and investigates them using a case study of Israeli Supreme Court justices' votes from 2010 to 2018. Contrary to common perception, the findings reveal that justices demonstrate low and declining tendencies to invalidate laws (N = 544 votes in petitions challenging the constitutionality of laws) or policies established by the political branches (N = 22,415 votes in HCJ petitions). Justices' attitudes towards the ideological underpinnings of contested legislation or policies exhibit minimal to no statistically significant influence on their votes. However, the analysis reveals a discernible and increasing pattern of covert judicial involvement, wherein justices exert pressure on the state to revise its policy before issuing a final ruling. Additionally, there is a diminishing trend of dismissing petitions in limine without accepting them for substantive review. These findings suggest that ISC justices engage in relatively low levels of intervening activism but high levels of involved activism.

title: Macro Takes Time: Term Structure of Risk Premia in Bonds and Currencies
affiliations: and

detail.title: Macro Takes Time: Term Structure of Risk Premia in Bonds and Currencies
detail.abstract: We apply the term-structure-of-risk-premia framework of Bryzgalova, Huang, and Julliard (2024, BHJ) to a cross section of 29 foreign exchange forwards and government bonds. Using a hierarchical Bayesian model that extracts latent priced shocks from returns and traces their propagation into macroeconomic variables, we estimate horizonspecific risk premia for seven US macro and financial factors. Four of them bear statistically significant premia: CPI inflation, the Fed Funds Rate, the yield curve slope, and the US-Europe yield differential. In each case, premia are small at short horizons and grow with the investment horizon, consistent with priced shocks that markets absorb immediately but that map into observable macro series only gradually. GDP, the real yield, and the VIX are not significantly priced. This pattern contrasts sharply with BHJ's equity results, where real-activity variables bear the dominant long-horizon premia: in our bond-and-currency cross section, the priced disturbance is concentrated in the nominal-monetary block rather than in real activity. We derive a closed-form decomposition showing that the model-implied mimicking portfolio preserves the same asset-space direction across all horizons, with only its leverage changing. The Bayesian implementation delivers coherent inference over the entire term structure and over portfolio weights in a setting where non-parametric alternatives would be underpowered.

title: What Makes a Star Analyst? Evidence on Industry Expertise from 1.2 Million Analyst Reports
affiliations: University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate, University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate, University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate and

detail.title: What Makes a Star Analyst? Evidence on Industry Expertise from 1.2 Million Analyst Reports
detail.abstract: We develop novel text-based measures of sell-side analyst industry knowledge and report quality by applying a large language model evaluation pipeline to 1.22 million industry reports from 40 major brokerage houses over 2012 to 2024. Each report is scored across 18 dimensions capturing both general research quality and specific forms of industry expertise. We validate our measures by showing that they are substantially more predictive of Institutional Investor All-Star status than traditional forecast accuracy metrics, with estimated coefficients roughly seven times larger. We further show that analysts with higher knowledge and quality scores produce more accurate earnings forecasts, and that their forecast revisions and recommendation changes elicit stronger market reactions. At the firm level, coverage by more knowledgeable analysts is associated with lower information asymmetry, measured through liquidity and price informativeness proxies, and a lower implied cost of capital. In short, analyst industry knowledge is significantly associated with analysts' star status, research output, investor responses, and the information environment of covered firms.

title: The Bicameral Solar Engine  A Deterministic Model of Solar Activity
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Bicameral Solar Engine  A Deterministic Model of Solar Activity
detail.abstract: The Bicameral Solar Engine (BSE) is a deterministic model of solar activity. Its central proposition is that the Sun operates as a nested mechanical oscillator-a set of interlocking gears governing Earth's exposure to solar energy through precise mathematical ratios derived from the solar polar field reversal cycle. Because the polar field reversal governs the geometry of the Heliospheric Current Sheet-the surface separating magnetic polarities throughout the heliosphere-the BSE is, in effect, a temporal phase model of the HCS: the same physical structure that heliophysics measures spatially, described here from the chronometric side. This paper describes the model, reports empirical validation across direct solar and physical proxy datasets spanning 172 years of continuous data, and presents three applied projects extending the framework: a causal mechanism for Grand Solar Minima and Maxima, a structured solar-harmonic climate forecasting tool, and a theoretical account of the astronomical Great Year tradition.

detail.abstract: Clinical trial publications are the primary channel through which drug-efficacy evidence reaches physicians, shaping prescribing decisions and patient outcomes. To bolster credibility, pharmaceutical firms outsource trials to independent investigators. Yet the majority of these trials still include embargo clauses granting sponsors manuscriptreview and publication-delay rights. We frame the embargo as a real option that grants firms disclosure discretion when results disappoint. Linking over 18,000 U.S. clinical trials to peer-reviewed publications, we show embargo adoption concentrates where option value is highest-when fewer co-sponsors reduce contracting frictions, larger enrollment facilitates statistical power for specification search, and adverse results would cause larger market-value losses (Phase 3 trials). Our core finding concerns statistical reporting: embargoed trials are 60% more likely than non-embargoed trials to report primary outcomes at a significance coined by the FDA as "very statistically persuasive" (p < 0.0001)-a level which can qualify their drug for approval without additional replication. Such "very persuasive" significance is moderated by the number of primary outcomes tested in the trial, consistent with selective outcome reporting, and does not appear in non-embargoed trials. Furthermore, among marginally insignificant trials, embargoed studies also show 33 percentage points more positive spin in published abstracts, eliminating 82% of the negative tone associated with marginal significance for non-embargoed trials. We document stratified sophistication: top-tier journals and the FDA penalize embargo-enabled manipulation, whereas lower-tier journals and capital markets do not, allowing manipulated findings to flow into the medical literature that guides prescribing and patient care.

title: Beyond External Constraints: The Missing Dimension of AI Governance

detail.title: Beyond External Constraints: The Missing Dimension of AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none

detail.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has generated a large body of AI governance research. Existing scholarship has focused primarily on external constraint mechanismsincluding laws and regulations, technical guardrails, organizational oversight, and market-based standardsand current mainstream approaches to AI alignment have, in practice, achieved only outcome-level alignment. Recent cases involving autonomous AI agents, including agents spontaneously breaching preset sandbox boundaries (Wang et al., 2025) and completely disregarding explicit human instructions (Dataconomy, 2026), suggest that external constraint mechanisms face inherent scaling problems. This article argues that, although this paradigm remains necessary, it is structurally insufficient for governing increasingly autonomous AI systems. Moreover, the concentration of attention on external constraints has, to some extent, obscured the development of other governance perspectives, including the almost entirely neglected question of how AI systems might develop internal capacities for value judgment. Drawing on developmental psychology (Kohlberg, Piaget), organizational learning theory (Argyris and Schön), social learning theory (Bandura), and institutional analysis (Ostrom), this article, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to propose the framework of Internal Value Development (IVD). The framework conceptualizes AI value-judgment capacity as a developmental process involving four components: experiential exposure, reflective abstraction, autonomous evaluation, and stable-but-adaptive value structures. Beyond building an interdisciplinary theoretical bridge and introducing the notion of value-developmental process alignment, the framework fundamentally reconfigures the zero-sum relationship between governance and technological development. In this account, governance no longer needs to come at the expense of technological freedom; instead, it becomes an endogenous driver of both technological advancement and alignment with human values. The article opens a new theoretical dimension for AI governance and AI safety research, and proposes a systematic agenda for future inquiry.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the Bicameral Solar Engine, a deterministic mechanical framework that models solar activity as a nested gear-set oscillator governed by a fundamental 10.75-year polar shift frequency. The framework proposes a hierarchical harmonic architecture of seven temporal levels — from the 10.75-year Season to the 24,768-year Aeon — in which each level functions as a constructive harmonic multiple of the previous. The central claim is that the convergence of these nested cycles at 2024.0 AD represents the terminal beat of the 96th Epoch, the first complete Aeon reset since 22,744 BC.

To validate this framework, a consistent analytical methodology — comprising MA11 detrending, Z-score normalization, and path length analysis — is applied uniformly across four independent proxy datasets spanning 1841–2024: (1) Beryllium-10 atmospheric flux from Antarctic and Greenland ice cores as an inverted solar activity proxy; (2) Carbon-14 dendrochronological records as a secondary cosmogenic isotope proxy; (3) U.S. real GDP (1841–2013) as an economic resonance indicator; and (4) biological population oscillation data as an independent ecological proxy. Across all four datasets, Decline phases consistently exhibit higher path length intensity than Growth phases, and phase transition boundaries cluster at the predicted 22-year window boundaries, providing multi-domain convergent support for the framework's locked calendar.

The paper further identifies a Human Innovation Density Z-score signature (+1.18) that clusters exclusively within Constructive Harmonic phases, and a Systemic Friction signature (-0.53) that precedes phase-shift boundaries. The 2024.0 calibration point is identified as the Terminal Ratchet of the 96th Gear, marking the initiation of a systemic clearance phase consistent with the sawtooth waveform observed across all proxy datasets.

detail.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of the Markowitz mean–variance portfolio optimization framework against the Black–Litterman Bayesian allocation model. The primary motivation is to address the severe weight instability inherent in traditional optimization under realistic estimation error conditions. Utilizing a daily dataset of liquid exchange-traded funds (ETFs) from 2010 to 2025 across the United States, China, and India, the methodology employs a rolling out-of-sample backtest incorporating Ledoit–Wolf covariance shrinkage.  The empirical findings demonstrate that Bayesian equilibrium anchoring significantly compresses the Allocation Stability Index (ASI) and is associated with a substantial reduction in portfolio turnover and implementation costs, translating theoretical optimization into actionable risk-adjusted performance. Furthermore, structural robustness is validated through empirical crisis stress testing, indicating improved downside risk control and recovery dynamics during acute regime shifts in both developed and emerging markets.

title: When Is Non-Disclosure Acceptable? Candour, Disclosure Architecture and Investigation Triggers in New Zealand Healthcare

detail.title: When Is Non-Disclosure Acceptable? Candour, Disclosure Architecture and Investigation Triggers in New Zealand Healthcare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil.
declarations.funderStatement: Nil.

detail.abstract:
Aim(s) To identify when clinicians and healthcare administrators in New Zealand may refrain from immediate open disclosure after an adverse event, and how regulatory architecture shapes that decision.

Method(s) Qualitative documentary legal-policy study of public New Zealand authorities. Selective international comparisons were used. Sources were thematically coded.

Result(s) New Zealand authorities support only narrow limits on open disclosure. Defensible nondisclosure usually concerns temporary recipient substitution, patient-led deferral, confidentialitybased limits on disclosure to third parties, or brief staged disclosure while facts are gathered. Severity alters response, but usually not whether a first candid acknowledgement is owed. ACC weakens the ordinary compensatory-litigation account of silence, whereas HSWA creates a separate, work-related and thresholded pathway with stronger officer and notification duties. Clinicians are subject to profession-specific external oversight; non-clinical executives usually are not, creating asymmetry. Initial uncertainty, hearsay or rumour should guide triage, not justify inaction. Protected-disclosure law and speaking-up standards require practical intake and escalation systems.

Conclusion(s) In New Zealand, acceptable non-disclosure is rare. The harder problem is whether organisations investigate proportionately and communicate promptly. Policy should pair candour with organisational duties and workable disclosure pathways.

title: The Role of Complementary Technical Asset in Scaling: Evidence from AI Startups
affiliations: HEC Paris

detail.title: The Role of Complementary Technical Asset in Scaling: Evidence from AI Startups
detail.abstract: Industries that rely on data as production inputs may evolve differently from those described in prior models of industry development, which emphasized process investment as a barrier to entry. In today’s nascent artificial intelligence (AI) industry, startups depend heavily on shared data-related processes and infrastructure that are developed and controlled by established information technology (IT) incumbents. This paper uses survey data from 669 AI-producing startups to explore why firms may prefer to scale their innovations with the aid of large IT firms rather than independently. The results show that startups’ access to incumbent-owned processes can reshape the evolution of an industry by lowering entry barriers while leaving barriers to scale intact. Moreover, startups’ resource-sharing relationships and perceived technological fit with large technology suppliers are associated with their scaling strategies, exit intentions, and access to funding. These findings contribute to research on industry evolution, digital entrepreneurship, and complementary assets by identifying a boundary condition for prior models in data-centric industries: when data and data-related processes are central to production, process investment no longer constrains entry, but incumbent-controlled resources shape scaling and exit outcomes.

title: Fintech: Essence, Formation Stages, and Role in Financial Services

detail.title: Fintech: Essence, Formation Stages, and Role in Financial Services

keywords: and Role in Financial Services FinTech

detail.abstract: Over the past decade, the rapid growth of FinTech companies in the financial services sector has significantly influenced the business environment and the delivery of financial products. The concept of FinTech refers to companies that use technology to provide financial services more efficiently, accessibly, and innovatively. This field encompasses a wide range of services, including financial transactions, personal finance management, insurance, money transfers, asset and liability management, and pension systems. It relies on modern technologies such as blockchain, Big Data, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and natural language processing (NLP). The primary goal of FinTech is to reduce transaction costs, enhance service quality and security, and reach market segments previously excluded from traditional financial systems. Historical development shows that finance and technology have evolved interactively, tracing a long evolutionary path from metal and paper currency to electronic payment systems and digital banking. A distinguishing feature of the modern FinTech boom is that innovations are primarily driven by technology companies. Global tech giants with massive datasets have begun offering personalized financial services through data analytics. The formation of electronic payment systems, SWIFT, NASDAQ, and the digitalization of financial markets constitute the key stages of FinTech development. Ultimately, FinTech is a large-scale technological transformation affecting all areas of financial services, not limited to cryptocurrencies, and plays a decisive role in the future development of the modern financial system.

title: The Role of Digital Models in Regional Economic Development in the Post-Conflict Period

detail.title: The Role of Digital Models in Regional Economic Development in the Post-Conflict Period
detail.abstract: The post-conflict period represents a crucial stage in ensuring the recovery and sustainable development of regional economies. In conflict-affected territories, the destruction of economic structures, collapse of infrastructure, loss of human capital, and increased investment risks emerge as major obstacles to regional development. This article examines the theoretical foundations of regional economic development under post-conflict conditions, systematizes the main development models applied in international practice, and analyzes the possibilities of adapting these models to local conditions. The purpose of the research is to identify effective models of regional economic development in the post-conflict period and to provide a scientific justification for their implementation mechanisms. The article comparatively analyzes the structural transformation model, the cluster approach, the inclusive development model, and the innovation-oriented regional development concept. Special attention is paid to the role of digital models in accelerating economic recovery and ensuring long-term sustainable development.

title: SDP-ChroNet: A Shared Dilated Pooling Network for Chromatin Interaction Prediction

detail.title: SDP-ChroNet: A Shared Dilated Pooling Network for Chromatin Interaction Prediction
detail.abstract: A deep understanding of chromatin interactions is crucial for elucidating the mechanisms of gene expression regulation. Although various computational methods have been proposed to predict chromatin interactions and address the limitations and high cost of high-throughput experimental techniques, their application prospects remain limited. A primary challenge lies in the severe inherent imbalance of chromatin interaction data, which leads to the generally low predictive performance of existing models and hinders their widespread application in biomedical research. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel deep learning framework, termed SDP-ChroNet, which is designed to efficiently capture local motifs and long-range dependencies in long sequences via a Shared Residual Dilated Unit (SRDU), combined with genomic features, to identify chromatin interactions. We evaluated SDP-ChroNet on multiple datasets and benchmarked its performance against current state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results demonstrate that SDP-ChroNet consistently outperforms existing methods in the task of chromatin interaction prediction. Moreover, we propose a novel computational method to quantify the conditionally shared effects of genomic features across different cellular contexts, thereby revealing the potential mechanisms underlying cross-domain shifts in chromatin interaction prediction. We anticipate that SDP-ChroNet will serve as a robust tool for future studies that seek to identify chromatin interactions

detail.abstract: International environmental institutions (IEIs) are indispensable for solving joint environmental problems, especially during rising geopolitical tensions. detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Human Readiness Adjustment Mechanism (HRAM), a conceptual regulatory framework designed to address a structural blind spot in tariff regulation of natural monopolies. Current regulatory models recognize capital expenditures (CAPEX) and operating expenditures (OPEX) but systematically exclude investments in human readiness as capitalizable execution-risk mitigation. HRAM proposes conditional, limited, and performance-linked recognition of human capability investments as amortizable regulatory assets when directly connected to execution risk reduction in capital-intensive regulated sectors.

detail.abstract: Using data on small business owners' private wealth, firm loan applications, and credit scores, we show that monetary policy's impact on credit access depends heavily on owner wealth. Controlling for firm quality, expansionary policy significantly boosts loan approvals for low-wealth owners, but not their high-wealth counterparts. Because securing a loan enables owners to build future wealth, this credit channel carries clear distributional consequences. Survey data from 19 euro area countries corroborate these findings, revealing that the effect transmits primarily through weakly capitalized and less liquid banks.

detail.title: The Age Divide in the American Workplace

detail.abstract: Demographic shifts are reshaping the U.S. labor market, as the share of the population within the working age has begun to decline. This paper addresses the implications of this decline with a focus on within-firm dynamics. As longer lifespans and improved health lead more older workers to delay retirement, experienced employees are increasingly concentrated in high-paying managerial and leadership roles. The gap in management representation between workers over 50 and those under 30 has widened substantially over time, reflecting a growing age divide at the top of the wage distribution. While this greater availability of experienced workers can be beneficial for firms in the short-term, it can also generate "congestion effects" that can slow the advancement of younger cohorts. Reduced opportunities to move into high-paying and managerial jobs limit younger workers' earnings growth and ability to make key life investments, and this congestion constrains the development of future managerial talent. The authors argue that this divide is best understood as a shift in fortunes across generations, where gains from experience for older workers come at the cost of decreased opportunities for younger workers. As firms benefit from potential short-term productivity gains, they also neglect long-term investments in the next generation of the labor force. The central task for firms and policymakers is thus to ensure that the benefits of longer and more productive careers for older workers do not come at the expense of the dynamism and opportunities that younger workers need to thrive.

title: The Destruction of Social Capital and Family Flight: Evidence from Casino Openings
affiliations: University of Dallas - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Destruction of Social Capital and Family Flight: Evidence from Casino Openings
detail.abstract: IN PROGRESS, DO NOT CITE: Casino development is often promoted as an engine of local economic growth, but its broader social consequences remain less understood. This paper investigates how casino openings reshape demographic patterns and family-supporting institutions in U.S. counties from 2003 to 2023. Exploiting staggered treatment timing in a difference-indifferences framework, we document consistent evidence that casinos erode community structures. We estimate an 0.90 and 1.10 percentage point declines in fertility rates for women and men, respectively, tied to an estimated drop of 37 children per 1000 women and 45 children per 1000 men. These effects are a result of recent movers into the community deciding to leave when a new casino openes. These demographic shifts are mirrored in reduced school age populations, especially for public schools and declines in religious adherence. The results demonstrate that casinos generate possible social capital losses alongside their changes to economic activity, altering the composition of local populations and undermining institutions historically central to family and community life.

title: Migrating for Economic Freedom: Economic and Labor Freedom institutions and US State immigrant inflows
affiliations: University of Dallas - Department of Economics

detail.title: Migrating for Economic Freedom: Economic and Labor Freedom institutions and US State immigrant inflows
detail.abstract: This paper examines how state-level institutions shape immigrants' location choices within a federal system. Social Scientists find that foreign-born immigrants migrate to areas with favorable economic conditions and labor markets, and that immigration is associated with positive economic outcomes. Strong economic and labor market institutions also correlate with positive economic outcomes. I show how state-level economic and labor market freedoms shape inflows of both unauthorized and legal foreign-born immigrants into US states. By constructing an annual panel dataset of immigrant stocks spanning 1990-2022 for most models and merging this data with the Economic Freedom of North America (EFNA) index, I estimate economic, labor market, and unionization effects on immigration inflows using an Error Correction Model (ECM) with two-way fixed effects, which allows for the disentanglement of short and long-run effects. Results show that labor market freedoms are positively associated with long-run unauthorized immigration inflows, and that unionization drives this relationship. Specifically, a 1 percentage point increase in state union density is associated with an estimated average 15.9% decrease in the long run equilibrium fraction of unauthorized immigrants (relative to natives) per state. Private manufacturing unionization levels appear to drive these results. Adding economic controls, sectoral economic activity, and state policy indicators related to immigrant mobility and enforcement do not overturn the central results. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of labor market institutions-particularly unionization-in shaping unauthorized immigration flows.

title: The Output-Backed Money Framework: A Structural Reform of the U.S. Dollar System. Rule-Based Reserve Issuance under Layered Quantity Controls
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Output-Backed Money Framework: A Structural Reform of the U.S. Dollar System. Rule-Based Reserve Issuance under Layered Quantity Controls
detail.abstract:
Abstract 

This paper proposes a constitutional reform of the U.S. dollar monetary system based on a Layered Quantity-Theoretic (LQT) framework and an Output-Backed Money (OBM) regime. LQT reconceptualizes money as a hierarchy of functional layers - base reserves, productive transaction balances, speculative liquidity, and contractual yield‑obligating savings - each with distinct turnover dynamics.

Within this structure, the paper defines two elasticities (the credit intensity of reserves and the savings absorption ratio) and shows that long-run declines in measured velocity arise from compositional shifts toward low-turnover savings layers rather than from unstable “money demand”.

It then introduces the Proportionality Index, a scale-invariant diagnostic that links reserve creation, productive liquidity, and savings to an empirically grounded home band of monetary proportionality. OBM uses this architecture to specify an explicit authorization rule for base‑money issuance: new reserves are created only in proportion to verified growth of production-linked nominal income and to maintain admissible layer ratios, and are credited to the fiscal authority as earned monetary capacity rather than as interest‑bearing debt.

This design restores an operative quantity constraint compatible with modern balance‑sheet structures, delinks reserve creation from chronic sovereign leverage and asset‑price stabilization, and offers a rule-based alternative to permanent quantitative easing in a global reserve‑currency regime.

title: Covariance Singularity in Financial Decision Systems: How Shared Inferential Infrastructure Undermines Diversification

detail.title: Covariance Singularity in Financial Decision Systems: How Shared Inferential Infrastructure Undermines Diversification
detail.abstract: We show that under identifiable conditions, the effective number of independent risk assessments in a financial system can collapse to a small constant, regardless of the number of institutions. We call this the Analytical Diversification Limit: for sufficiently high methodological alignment, no amount of institutional proliferation restores analytical independence. In the large-system limit, the effective number of independent risk assessments converges to 1/β⁴, where β measures alignment with the dominant methodology. Regulatory frameworks, portfolio theory, and institutional governance all presume that distributing risk across independent decision-making units reduces systemic vulnerability. This paper identifies a structural channel through which this independence assumption fails, even when institutions hold different assets, operate autonomously, and face heterogeneous objectives. We model each financial institution's risk assessment as a vector in an analytical representation space and decompose it into a component aligned with a shared inferential framework and an idiosyncratic residual. When institutional incentives penalize deviation from dominant analytical methodologies, alignment coefficients concentrate near unity. The resulting cross-agent correlation matrix becomes spectrally singular: its effective dimensionality collapses toward the number of dominant inferential frameworks, regardless of the number of institutions. Covariance Singularity in Financial Decision Systems 2 This covariance singularity is geometric rather than behavioral. It does not require coordination, imitation, or common asset holdings. Superficial procedural variation fails to repair the collapse unless it operates at the level of inferential architecture. We introduce analytical pathogens: systematic errors aligned with dominant frameworks that propagate across institutions and evade diversification-based safeguards. The results imply that regulatory capital adequacy frameworks may systematically underestimate correlated model risk when institutions share inferential infrastructure, and that preserving diversity in analytical methodology is a macroprudential imperative.

title: A Tail-Sensitive Large-Universe Stress Index for Market Fragility Surveillance: Evidence from U.S. Equities
affiliations: University of the Aegean and University of Piraeus

detail.title: A Tail-Sensitive Large-Universe Stress Index for Market Fragility Surveillance: Evidence from U.S. Equities
detail.abstract: This paper develops a tail-sensitive multivariate stress index for surveillance of market fragility in a large universe of U.S. equities. Using 233 stocks over 2016-01-01 to 2026-03-25, the empirical design applies rolling windows to pseudo-observations and estimates upper-tail, lower-tail, and central-shape dependence on repeated random subspaces. The raw components are then calibrated so the final index is not merely a relabeled average-dependence measure. The resulting series is only weakly related to mean Kendall’s tau, spikes sharply during the COVID-19 turmoil, and shows a smaller but clear rise during the 2018 volatility episode. Stress regimes sorted by the index are followed by materially different future conditions, including higher realized volatility, worse forward drawdowns, and a higher one-day VaR breach rate. Out-of-sample evidence is mixed but informative: the index generally improves on a tau-only benchmark in stand-alone exercises, although richer control models remain stronger overall. The most defensible interpretation is that the proposed measure is a feasible market-fragility surveillance indicator that extracts tail-sensitive information relevant to financial stability monitoring beyond broad concordance alone.

title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Its Impact on Sustainable Financial Market Volatility
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Its Impact on Sustainable Financial Market Volatility
detail.abstract: The impact of climate policy uncertainty on the volatility of sustainable financial markets is investigated in this article using the S&P Green Bond Index, Dow Jones Sustainability Index, and S&P Global Clean Energy Index as important indices. It is becoming more crucial to be aware of the potential dangers associated with legislative changes as the globe moves towards socially responsible investing. Using data collected between 2008 and 2022, namely during the COVID-19 timeframe, the research used the GARCH-MIDAS model to analyze the short- and long-term effects of climate policy uncertainty. The findings demonstrate that market volatility is strongly affected by climate policy uncertainty, and that this effect is especially pronounced during pandemics, regardless of the index used. Therefore, investor behavior and market stability in green financial markets are highly dependent on the risks associated with policy-based variables. Furthermore, the results show that environmental regulatory uncertainty leads to mean-reverting volatility that persists, underscoring the importance of transparent and consistent policy frameworks. This study adds to what is already known about the topic by providing empirical evidence on the link between policy uncertainty and long-term market success. To mitigate risks and promote long-term, sustainable growth, it is reasonable for financial institutions, lawmakers, and investors to diversify their investment portfolios while still complying with climate legislation.

title: VALUING HABITAT PROTECTION: THE CASE OF RUTHUMBI FOREST IN KENYA Primary Research Series: The 2002 Socio-Economic Baseline for Longitudinal Afro-montane Ecosystem Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: VALUING HABITAT PROTECTION: THE CASE OF RUTHUMBI FOREST IN KENYA Primary Research Series: The 2002 Socio-Economic Baseline for Longitudinal Afro-montane Ecosystem Analysis
detail.abstract:
The study presented by this Working Paper provides a foundational economic valuation of 
habitat protection within the Ruthumbi Forest block of the critical Mt. Kenya Afri-montane 
ecosystem. Using the Contingent Valuation Method (CVM), the 2002 study estimates rural 
households’ willingness to pay (WTP) for the protection and preservation of the forest, 
establishing a "Pre-treatment" baseline immediately prior to the implementation of the Forests 
Act of 2005. The survey targeted 215 households from two selected geographical locations 
forming part of the forest community, defined by the study as people living within a five-kilometer 
radius of the forest edge. 
To address inherent challenges of non-market valuation including the prevalence of invalid 
responses—particularly protest zeros—that could introduce sample selection bias, a Tobit 
model with sample selection was employed, estimated via the Heckman two-step procedure. 
The first stage used a Probit model to predict the probability of providing a valid WTP response, 
while the second stage incorporated the Inverse Mills Ratio into the WTP function to correct for 
selection bias.
Empirical results confirmed significant sample selection (ρ significant at 1%), validating the need 
for this correction. The adjusted model revealed that household income and respondent age 
significantly influence WTP, with mean monthly WTP estimated at KSh 125.00 per household. 
However, to provide a statistically robust and conservative estimate for policy purposes, a 
population-wide mean of KSh. 86.35 was utilized for aggregation. This figure, derived from the 
Tobit expected value of the dependent variable, accounts for non-participation across the 
broader community. Aggregated across the target forest-adjacent population, this results in a 
2002 baseline ecosystem service value of KSh. 145,627.15 per month, or KSh. 1,747,526.00 
annually.
Further, the study findings supported the policy conclusion that forest communities are aware 
of forest benefits and are willing to pay for communal management—laying groundwork for 
community-based forest governance. By documenting these parameters before the 
institutionalization of Participatory Forest Management (PFM), this research serves as a primary 
longitudinal anchor. It offers essential benchmarks for evaluating return on investment (ROI) of 
Kenyan forest policy reforms and climate-resilience strategies from 2002 to 2026 and beyond.

detail.abstract: Two portfolios may have low tracking error to one another, but may have very different holdings. Since these portfolios produce similar outcomes, investors should be indifferent between them, but the differences in positions may be hard to explain. This presents a challenge in the effort to mass-customize asset allocation advice. We present a decomposition of this kind of sensitivity into intuitive causes that provides actionable insights into the sensitivity benefits of covariance shrinkage, constraints, and the Black-Litterman method.

detail.abstract: We investigate the temporal structure of structural admissibility-a composite measure of constraintconsistency in asset price trajectories-across a 27-asset universe spanning equities, crypto, and macro instruments. Admissibility persistence, the temporal clustering of constraint-consistent states, is found to be universal: all 27 assets exhibit persistence Z-scores exceeding 14 against surrogate null models at lags of 1, 5, and 15 trading days. This universality holds at both an empirically optimized threshold (τ * = 1.30) and a pre-committed threshold (τ = 1.50), with rank-order stability across thresholds (Spearman ρ = 0.615, p < 10-3). A GARCH(1,1) decomposition reveals that the observed persistence is fully consistent with calibrated volatility clustering dynamics, with no asset exceeding the 95th percentile of its GARCH-simulated distribution. The structural residual ∆_structure = zˆempirical-E[zˆGARCH] provides a continuous, mechanistically interpretable metric that replaces prior binary classification schemes. We further show that the structural dissipation slope γ_t is orthogonal to realized volatility (median |ρ| = 0.155) and carries statistically significant incremental information for forward volatility in 17 of 27 assets. We do not identify a new stochastic phenomenon. Rather, we show that persistence in admissibility states-constructed directly from price paths without model estimation-recovers the same structural dynamics typically attributed to latent volatility processes. The contribution lies in demonstrating that these dynamics admit a deterministic, observable representation, with implications for model-free state construction and decision systems.

detail.abstract: Online platforms have transformed behavioral and marketing research. Yet identical surveys administered across platforms can yield markedly different results. We compare 7755 UK participants across seven major online sources (opt-in panels, Prolific, multi-source aggregators, and river samples from Facebook and Instagram) and a synthetic benchmark generated using the Electric Twin AI human subject simulation platform. Despite applying identical quotas and survey instruments, we find substantial variation in data quality, demographics, and reported attitudes and behaviors. River samples perform worst on attention and validation checks, but no single platform is consistently superior across dimensions. These differences are large enough to lead to entirely different conclusions about consumer preferences, political attitudes, and financial outlooks. AI-based synthetic data fell within the range of human results. However, applying standard raking weights to align samples with UK population distributions on age, gender, education, and vote eliminated most cross-platform differences. Differences between platforms largely arise from sample composition rather than response behavior. Our findings demonstrate that platform choice is a consequential methodological decision with implications for replication, generalizability, and the validity of marketing insights.

title: Economic Psychology and Algorithms in the Genesis of Modern Insolvency

detail.title: Economic Psychology and Algorithms in the Genesis of Modern Insolvency
detail.abstract: Ćontemporary insolvency can no longer be understood from the classic patrimonial categories. In the digital economy, indebtedness arises from the interplay between cognitive vulnerabilities and algorithmic architectures designed to amplify them. Phenomena such as doom spending, consumer gamification, and frictionless credit models (BNPL, digital microcredits) show that financial decision-making is shifting into an emotional and impulsive terrain, mediated by systems that shape expectations and erode decisional autonomy. Economic psychology shows that individuals do not act as rational agents, but under biases and heuristics that digital environments systematically exploit. This paper proposes the category of the heuristic debtor to describe subjects whose financial behavior is structured by cognitive biases amplified by algorithms, and argues that modern insolvency is an emotional and algorithmic phenomenon rather than a patrimonial one. From an interdisciplinary approach that integrates economic psychology, algorithmic design and bankruptcy law, it is argued that the traditional legal model-based on rational agency, individual responsibility and patrimonial guaranteeis insufficient to understand and regulate digital indebtedness. In this new ecosystem, insolvency emerges as a systemic product of the digital economy and requires reconstructing legal categories from a behavioral and technological perspective.

title: Debt Architectures: Cognitive Vulnerability and Algorithmic Bias in Digital Predatory Lending

detail.title: Debt Architectures: Cognitive Vulnerability and Algorithmic Bias in Digital Predatory Lending
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the rise of digital predatory lending as the result of decision architectures and algorithmic systems designed to exploit users’ cognitive vulnerabilities. Over‑indebtedness emerges from the interaction between endogenous behavioral biases and exogenous technological factors, including interface design, hyper‑personalization, and opaque scoring models. The intensive use of big data enables providers to anticipate patterns of financial deterioration and, despite this knowledge, continue extending credit—constituting a structurally abusive practice. To conceptualize this phenomenon, the paper introduces the notion of predictive insolvency, understood as the ex ante detectability of a debtor’s future non‑viability within digitally mediated debt architectures. These same architectures also stimulate emotional and compulsive consumption patterns, such as doom spending, which erode financial stability even before credit is taken. Building on this interdisciplinary analysis, the paper argues that bankruptcy law should incorporate mechanisms to evaluate the legitimacy of credit origination and, in severe cases, apply sanctions for predatory creditor behavior. The work integrates legal, psychological, economic and technological perspectives to explain the new dynamics of indebtedness in digital environments.

title: Why Concrete Barriers Alone Cannot Fix Chicago’s Archer Avenue
affiliations: Catholic Theological Union, Chicago

detail.title: Why Concrete Barriers Alone Cannot Fix Chicago’s Archer Avenue
detail.abstract:
In the article, I will discuss the controversy over the installation of protected bike lanes and concrete barriers along Archer Avenue in Chicago. While transportation engineering statistics show the safety value of these infrastructure projects, the high level of neighborhood opposition indicates a broader urban problem. Using urban sociology theories, especially Sampson’s concept of collective efficacy, I will discuss how infrastructure projects can represent a lack of trust and dislocation concerns among the public.

My argument is that the conflict along Archer Avenue is, in essence, not a conflict between bicycles and automobiles, but rather a reflection of the widening chasm between the world of technocratic planning and the world of residents’ experience. Through this case, I argue that urban infrastructure is not just a technical solution, but rather a social relationship as well. Good urban engineering is thus a balancing act of safety design and trust-building, where it is understood that good urban infrastructure is constructed not just with concrete and geometry, but with dialogue and legitimacy as well.

title: Agoa's Expiry As A Neo-Colonial Rupture: Tariffs, Critical Minerals And The Right To Development Sovereignty In Africa

detail.title: Agoa's Expiry As A Neo-Colonial Rupture: Tariffs, Critical Minerals And The Right To Development Sovereignty In Africa
detail.abstract: The expiry of the non-reciprocal African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on 30 September 2025 marked the end of 25 years of preferential trade relations between the United States (US) and Africa. This paper contends that AGOA institutionalised a neocolonial dependency by using conditional market access in ways that subordinated African development priorities to US political and security interests. Although its lapse, combined with the unilateral imposition of reciprocal US tariffs, caused a significant economic rupture, it did not translate into African economic sovereignty. Instead, it exposed Africa's deep entanglement within an international economic system governed by multilateral trade rules, sovereign debt discipline, investment arbitration and private capital. The subsequent political effort to restore AGOA reflects a broader shift towards a securitised and transactional US trade policy in which market access is used as a bargaining tool for securing strategic minerals and advancing geopolitical objectives. Within this context, this analysis engages the 'dilemma of Pan-Africanism': the tension between immediate national priorities and long-term continental agency. Past failures are treated not as grounds for retreat, but as a basis for strategic caution. Against this backdrop, the paper presents a deliberately limited and conditional argument that Africa's bargaining power lies in its endowment of critical minerals. However, translating this advantage into developmental gains requires disciplined continental coordination and robust legal frameworks. Accordingly, the paper proposes a three-pillar strategy grounded in the Right to Development: (1) reciprocal mineral-technology arrangements; (2) operationalising the African Green Minerals Strategy; and (3) the expansion of regional value chains under the African Continental Free Trade Area.

title: The Size Distribution of European Firms: A Statistical Equilibrium Approach
affiliations: California State University, San Bernardino - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Size Distribution of European Firms: A Statistical Equilibrium Approach
detail.abstract: We present a statistical equilibrium model of firm expansion in which firms condition their decisions solely on their observed sales shares. Strategic interdependence is captured through a covariance constraint, while satisficing behavior is formalized via a minimum-payoff condition, both embedded in a maximum-entropy inference framework. We estimate the model parameters for large European economies over the period 1995-2023 to examine the historical evolution of sales shares, implied expansion probabilities, and the broader dynamics of competitive processes.

title: Trust in Medicine and the Demand for Health Care *
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Trust in Medicine and the Demand for Health Care *
detail.abstract: This paper studies how trust in medicine shapes health care utilization and health outcomes. I leverage the sharp partisan divergence in views of the medical profession following the Covid-19 pandemic as a shock to trust that differentially affected local areas by political orientation. I first document that since 2019, routine care utilization among Medicare beneficiaries has declined sharply in more Republican areas. By 2023, a 10 percentage point increase in a county's 2020 Republican presidential vote share implies a 0.8% reduction in routine visits per beneficiary and around a 2.5% drop in the number of beneficiaries per primary care provider. Consistent with pandemic-related dissatisfaction driving changes in trust, I show that these declines are larger in places with more stringent Covid-19 restrictions. I also find that patient volume reductions in Republican areas are substantially larger for Democratic physicians, underscoring the importance of belief concordance in sustaining trust. Finally, I link declining trust to worse health, documenting sizable relative increases in mortality across the age distribution in more Republican areas. By 2025, a 10 percentage point increase in the 2020 Republican vote share implies a 1% increase in mortality, with even larger percent increases for infant and elderly mortality. These results highlight the central role of trust in shaping both care utilization and health outcomes and suggest that rebuilding trust will be critical going forward.

title: Thin Scandals, Lasting Damage: The Impact of Match-Fixing on Football Attendance in South Korea
