detail.abstract: Financial Technology (FinTech) has brought significant changes to traditional banking operations worldwide. In India, innovations such as digital wallets, mobile banking, blockchain, artificial intelligence, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) have transformed the delivery and accessibility of financial services. This paper presents a systematic review of existing literature to examine the impact of FinTech innovations on the Indian banking system. The study is based on secondary data collected from peer-reviewed journals, Reserve Bank of India reports, and other credible academic sources. The findings indicate that FinTech adoption has enhanced operational efficiency, improved customer experience, and promoted financial inclusion among Indian banks. However, challenges related to cybersecurity risks, regulatory compliance, and high implementation costs persist. The study concludes that FinTech offers substantial opportunities for the banking sector, provided that banks adopt robust risk management practices and align technological strategies with regulatory frameworks.

title: A Legal Theory of State-Owned Enterprises
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: A Legal Theory of State-Owned Enterprises
detail.abstract: Why are state-owned enterprises (SOEs) so prevalent in China, and why do they dominate certain sectors more than others? While current studies provide various political and economic explanations, they fall short of fully accounting for the distribution of SOEs across industries in China. For example, in sectors like infrastructure, the government has actively sought to attract private investment, yet SOEs continue to play a major role. This book introduces a legal theory of SOEs, arguing that the prevalence of SOEs in some sectors in China can be explained by the high regulatory costs associated with regulating the enterprises. Regulatory costs affect state ownership through both the supply-side and demand-side mechanisms. On the supply side, the state would continue to maintain and supply SOEs if it perceives it necessary to maintain control. On the demand side, private investors would refrain from making investment to meet the market demand if they expect the state to frequently adjust regulation that negatively affect their property interests. Therefore, the success of SOE reform is closely linked to the development of robust legal and regulatory institutions.

title: How to Properly Measure Moral Universalism
affiliations: Université de Poitiers, Philosophy Department and Montpellier Business School

detail.title: How to Properly Measure Moral Universalism
detail.abstract: Enke et al. (2022) have introduced the interesting concept of “moral universalism” as “the extent to which people exhibit the same level of altruism and trust toward strangers as toward in-group members”. We argue that concerns arise both regarding the theoretical clarity of the concept and the extent to which it genuinely measures what it purports to measure. We distinguish between four reasons for which some economic considerations are not eliminated as expected, due to confounds related to purchasing power disparities, wealth heterogeneity, and relative socio-economic status, and one reason related to the soundness of the distinction between in-group and out-group in the instructions. We conclude by proposing a revised version of the experimental instructions. Even if the past empirical results would have been unchanged by our proposal, we claim that the revised instructions we propose should be used in the future.

title: Attention to Monetary Policy
affiliations: Yonsei University, Yonsei University - School of Economics and Yonsei University, Graduate School

detail.title: Attention to Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: We develop a Google Trends-based Monetary Policy Attention (MPA) index to measure the intensity of public focus on monetary policy. While conducting a series of validation analyses, we find that the MPA index specifically captures search intensity related to monetary policy rather than general economic noise; the index rises significantly with inflation and monetary policy-related uncertainty, while remaining unresponsive to broader economic policy uncertainty. Using a state-dependent local projection method, we examine how the effectiveness of monetary policy shocks varies with the level of attention. We find that during periods of high MPA, monetary policy tightening-even when devoid of signaling components-leads to a divergence between prices and inflation expectations, ultimately attenuating the monetary policy transmission mechanism. These results suggest that high states of public attention can paradoxically hinder the central bank's ability to anchor inflation through traditional interest rate adjustments.

title: The COVID-19 Pandemic and Carbon Emissions: A Sectoral Analysis of India and Global Trends Against the Paris Agreement Targets

detail.title: The COVID-19 Pandemic and Carbon Emissions: A Sectoral Analysis of India and Global Trends Against the Paris Agreement Targets
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered an unprecedented contraction in global economic activity, producing a rare natural experiment for observing the relationship between human activity and carbon emissions. This paper examines sector-wise variation in CO2 emissions in India and globally during the pandemic year of 2020, using daily near-real-time data from the Carbon Monitor, and benchmarks observed changes against the 7.6% annual reduction target required under the Paris Climate Agreement to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees C. We find a global CO2 decline of 4.57% in 2020 relative to the 2019 baseline, substantially below the Paris-required threshold, and achieved only through the severe disruption of most economic activity. India's overall decline was steeper at 8.33%, driven disproportionately by the industrial sector (-13.92%) and domestic aviation (-45.71%), reflecting the comparative stringency of India's lockdown measures. Critically, emissions in most sectors had substantially recovered to pre-pandemic levels by the second half of 2020, while ground transportation and aviation showed sustained decline through year-end. The findings suggest that pandemic-induced emission reductions represent a temporary and structurally shallow disruption rather than a meaningful contribution to long-term decarbonization, and that achieving Paris targets will require sustained structural transformation across all major emitting sectors.

title: Narrative Infrastructure: Micro-Stories as the Constitutive Medium of Organizational Life

detail.title: Narrative Infrastructure: Micro-Stories as the Constitutive Medium of Organizational Life

declarations.ethicsApproval: no ethical issues
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This paper develops a new framework for understanding the role of stories in organizational life. It argues that organizations should not be understood primarily as settings in which leaders use storytelling instrumentally for persuasion, alignment, or change communication. Rather, they should be understood as systems that are continuously organized through micro-stories: small, circulating narrative forms through which organizational members interpret events, infer consequences, define local norms, and orient action. On that basis, the paper introduces the concept of narrative infrastructure to describe the distributed ecology of remembered episodes, cautionary tales, compressed references, and recurring story fragments that connect formal organizational arrangements with lived organizational reality. The paper makes four main contributions. First, it differentiates analytically among storytelling, narrative, and micro-stories, proposing microstories as a formally defined narrative unit distinguishable from scripts, schemas, norms, and rumors, and differentiates narrative infrastructure from the adjacent concept of antenarrative. Second, it shows that micro-stories perform cognitive, social, political, identity-related, and temporal functions in organizations, organized across individual and system levels, while also contributing to the reproduction of silence, fear, and tacit compliance. Third, it conceptualizes organizations as polyphonic story systems and argues that managers require a capability of narrative listening and curation, not only storytelling, in order to understand and influence such systems. Fourth, it shows that the infrastructural role of stories becomes especially consequential 1 I use AI as a research assistant and as an editor. in complex and chaotic environments, where formal categories and linear models provide insufficient guidance for coordinated action. The paper concludes by arguing that change is best understood not simply as the introduction of a better official narrative, but as a shift in the distribution of lived stories inside the organization. In this view, organizations are shaped less by the stories they publish than by the micro-stories their members trust, repeat, contest, and act upon.

detail.title: Heterogeneous Oligopolistic Multiproduct Firms and Business Cycle Dynamics
detail.abstract: A small number of large firms accounts for a substantial share of aggregate activity. We develop a tractable dynamic general-equilibrium model with heterogeneous granular firms, oligopolistic competition, endogenous product scope, and entry/exit, and show that it admits a unique Markov perfect equilibrium. We introduce a perturbation-based state reduction that delivers near-exact dynamic solutions for fat-tailed Pareto firm-size distributions. Firm-level shocks generate sizable aggregate fluctuations, mainly through the interaction of productivity and endogenous scope. Depending on whether shocks hit a dominant firm or many smaller firms, aggregate effects differ and the cyclicality of aggregate outcomes may reverse.

title: Suspicion and Communication
affiliations: University of Potsdam, University of Potsdam and

detail.title: Suspicion and Communication
detail.abstract: In this paper, we study how communication influences suspicion. The experiment uses a sender-receiver setup with a low probability of misaligned incentives for senders and receivers. We focus on the impact of open communication on the receivers' suspicion as measured by the size of the deviation from the senders' recommendation before and after the communication. Overall, communication substantially reduces suspicion, but some receivers become more suspicious during the communication. We disentangle these effects using machine learning methods to analyze the chat logs.

title: Co-creation and Multilevel-Governance: A Literature Report
affiliations: Université de Lausanne, University of Lausanne - Institut d'Etudes Politiques et Internationales,  and University of Berne

detail.title: Co-creation and Multilevel-Governance: A Literature Report
detail.abstract: As the EU advances its green and digital "twin transitions," public authorities seek governance approaches that link policy innovation with democratic legitimacy and delivery capacity. This report clarifies the meaning of co-creation in public governance and examines how it can be embedded within multilevel governance (MLG) so legitimacy, effectiveness, and inclusion reinforce one another across local, regional, national, and EU levels. Based on a narrative review of 111 publications, it shows that co-creation involves collaborative practices across the policy cycle-joint problem framing, design, implementation, and evaluation-engaging citizens, public institutions, civil-society organisations, businesses, and experts. While most practice occurs locally, higher tiers shape mandates, resources, standards, and digital platforms that enable or constrain experimentation and diffusion. The analysis identifies key benefits, including improved democratic legitimacy, knowledge quality, service and policy outcomes, and social cohesion, alongside risks such as tokenism, elite capture, representation gaps, digital exclusion, and limited scaling. When adequately supported, co-creation complements representative democracy and strengthens MLG's problem-solving capacity. title: A Multi-Model Analysis of the Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of Environmental Taxes and Renewable Energy on Decarbonization

detail.title: A Multi-Model Analysis of the Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of Environmental Taxes and Renewable Energy on Decarbonization
detail.abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of economic instruments in reducing carbon dioxide emissions in OECD countries. The focus is on renewable energy consumption and environmental taxation. Previous studies often report that both instruments reduce emissions. However, much of the literature relies on single econometric methods. This may overlook cross country heterogeneity, cross sectional dependence, and dynamic adjustment effects. To address these limitations, this study applies a multi model panel econometric framework using balanced OECD data from 2000 to 2022. Fixed effects, mean group, pooled mean group, and common correlated effects estimators are employed. These methods allow the identification of both short run and long run relationships while accounting for unobserved common factors. The results show that renewable energy consumption consistently and significantly reduces carbon dioxide emissions across all model specifications. The effect is stronger in the long run. In contrast, environmental tax revenue shows weak and unstable effects that depend on model choice. Economic growth does not have a significant long run impact on emissions. This suggests that efficiency gains and technological progress dominate scale effects in advanced economies. The findings highlight the importance of methodological robustness and support prioritizing renewable energy expansion over environmental taxation alone.

detail.abstract: In this Article we argue that contemporary antitrust disagreements are at heart conflicts between competing teleological frameworks, rather than disputes about economics, evidence, or enforcement attitude. We compares three influential approaches-consumer welfare, republican non-domination, and common good constitutionalism-as alternative second-best enforcement responses to uncertainty and epistemic limits. The analysis shows that these frameworks diverge along four dimensions: moral thickness, normative closure, sensitivity to ex-post injustice, and institutional design. While all reject first-best optimization, they propose sharply different ways of governing persistent disagreement. We conclude that antitrust regimes that institutionalize fallibility offer greater legitimacy and durability than those that seek to resolve uncertainty through authoritative moral settlement. Such regimes adopt a form of "republican welfarism," in which welfare remains the ultimate evaluative standard for rule selection, but its pursuit is constrained by a republican concern with non-domination. This constraint increases the legitimacy of welfare optimization where enforcement would generate arbitrary or irreversible harm.

title:
The Blind Side of the AI and Robotics Revolution:
When Productivity Forgets the People Who are Supposed to Buy the Output

detail.title:
The Blind Side of the AI and Robotics Revolution:
When Productivity Forgets the People Who are Supposed to Buy the Output
detail.abstract:
This article explores the systemic risks inherent in the current AI and robotics revolution, focusing on the "blind side" of the productivity miracle: the erosion of the demand engine. While global discourse frequently celebrates the efficiency gains and cost reductions brought about by automation, this paper argues that if these gains accrue primarily to capital while labor’s bargaining power and income share continue to decouple from productivity, the result is not a "golden age" but rather economic "involution." I define this phenomenon as a state of hyper-competition for shrinking margins, characterized by price wars and a consumption collapse driven by missing purchasing power rather than a lack of products. Drawing on historical parallels—including the economic stagnation of the later Roman Empire—and contemporary data regarding the global decline of the labor share, the article posits that a modern economy cannot be sustained by capital expenditure and asset re-pricing alone.

The central thesis emphasizes that labor serves a dual role: it is not merely a cost of production but the primary mechanism for distributing the purchasing power necessary to clear markets. When the "shared story" of a fair economic bargain weakens, the social and political coordination required to maintain complex systems begins to fail. The paper warns that without proactive strategies to ensure that the gains of AI are broadly distributed to maintain a robust consumer class, the widening imbalance between production capacity and household income will lead to structural deflation, political breakage, and the eventual snapping of the social contract.

title: Job Search, Job Amenities, and the Gender Pay Gap
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, University of Zurich - Department of Economics and Princeton University

detail.title: Job Search, Job Amenities, and the Gender Pay Gap

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-05
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies gender gaps in labor-market outcomes, with a focus on job ladder dynamics. We show that women experience substantially lower wage growth conditional on prior wages despite nearly identical job-to-job transition rates for men and women. To reconcile these observations, we document gender differences in the valuation of nonwage job amenities and in job search behavior, and develop a multi-dimensional job-ladder model with endogenous search effort where workers value both wages and amenities. The model allows for gender heterogeneity in separation rates, search effort, the value of nonemployment, amenity valuations, and bargaining power, enabling a joint analysis of gender wage and employment gaps. A quantitative decomposition shows that differences in preferences for nonwage amenities account for nearly 40 percent of the gender pay gap. Differences in the value of nonemployment and bargaining power explain most of the remainder, with only a limited role for differences in separation rates and search behavior. Finally, we show that increases in job amenities-such as the expansion of remote work-raise the gender wage gap while reducing gender differences in employment.

title: Socially-Minded Investors and Corporate Behavior
affiliations: Columbia University - Law School and University of California, Davis - School of Law

detail.title: Socially-Minded Investors and Corporate Behavior

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 916/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Many equity investors are concerned with the world’s worsening social and environmental problems and are losing faith in the capacity of political institutions to respond. Where corporate behavior is contributing to these problems, these investors would, at least if fully informed as to costs and benefits involved, favor corrective changes even where that would lessen their investment returns. Two important questions arise: (1) given existing law, are such willing-to-sacrifice equity investors currently affecting firm behavior; and (2) should there be legal reform that makes firms more sensitive to these willing-to-sacrifice investors’ preferences? This Article seeks to answer these two questions, applying the teachings of corporate governance and financial economics. We go back to first principles to explore, relative to the politics of governmental regulation, this alternative way of harnessing people’s other-regarding values to improve social welfare.

Under current corporate governance arrangements, a firm’s business decisions are, in the first instance, the product of its managers, not its shareholders. If willing-to-sacrifice investors are to have any effect on firm behavior, it must be through some indirect means. One possible channel is to elect directors who pledge to make the firm conform to these investors’ wishes. A second is through these investors’ impact on the workings of the incentive structure within which the firm’s managers operate. A third possible channel—identity investing—involves these investors confining their stock portfolios to firms whose social behavior they approve, thereby affecting share prices in ways that incentivize managers to choose the approved behavior.

Theory, we show, predicts that under current law, willing-to-sacrifice equity investors will not significantly affect firm behavior through either of the first two channels, and we see little evidence to the contrary. As for the third, theory suggests that identity investing will have some impact on share prices. Empirical evidence is mixed as to whether the effect is currently large enough to incentivize managers of excluded firms to significantly change their behavior.

Should there be legal reform that makes the system more sensitive than now to the preferences of willing-to-sacrifice investors? Some scholars have championed allowing binding shareholder votes on individual business decisions to increase this sensitivity. The upside is that allowing such votes might sometimes alter corporate behavior in socially useful ways. This upside is likely more than counterbalanced by the downsides. Specifically, all vote-based choice systems, whether public or private, expend resources and political energy in informing and mobilizing voters, and require these voters’ time and effort in response. The reform would divert such resources and effort from the public political process, one where, because of the scale of impact, results can be attained more efficiently. Moreover, to give managers the discretion needed to implement the results of such a shareholder vote, their incentive structure needs to be made less constraining in ways that would simultaneously allow managers to alter firm behavior simply to benefit themselves.

Modifying securities and pension law offers an at least modestly more promising path forward. Mandating disclosure of a firm’s social impacts, for example, would facilitate more identity investing, with its resulting impact on corporate behavior through its effect on the firm’s share price. The difficult question, one worthy of experimentation to answer, is whether that impact would be great enough to justify such disclosure’s considerable costs.

detail.abstract: African economies depend heavily on primary commodity exports and external financing, making their financial markets sensitive to global trade shocks. This study quantifies the effects of the Trump-era tariff wars on African financial markets by examining the responses of ten currencies and five stock markets. We find heterogeneous but measurable reactions across asset classes. During the first tariff episode, most currencies depreciated by an average of 2-3 percent against the US dollar, while the second episode was associated with appreciations of about 5-6 percent, partly reflecting uncertainty-driven US dollar weakness. Stock market responses were generally muted, with statistically insignificant gains in most cases, except for notable losses of about 5.1 percent in Kenya during the first shock and significant gains of roughly 11 percent in South Africa during the second. Overall, the findings suggest that African financial markets react heterogeneously to global tariff shocks, with exchange rates exhibiting broader sensitivity than equity markets. The results carry important implications for policymakers and investors in managing external vulnerability and portfolio risk.

title: Railroads and the Silver Shoes of Populism: The Rise and Fall of the People’s Party in 19th-Century America
affiliations: Bocconi University, Bocconi University and Bocconi University

detail.title: Railroads and the Silver Shoes of Populism: The Rise and Fall of the People’s Party in 19th-Century America

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The People's Party is the only major populist movement in American history that was quickly reabsorbed by mainstream parties. We study the main trigger of its risetechnological disruption from railroad expansion-and discuss its dissolution in light of the conceptual framework we develop and test empirically. We construct a novel county-level measure of Technological Disruption Exposure (TDE) that captures the change in competitive pressure each county faced from all other counties, driven by railroad-induced reductions in transportation costs between 1870 and 1890. TDE positively predicts People's Party vote share in the 1894 congressional elections: a one standard deviation increase raises Populist support by nearly 3 percentage points. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect is concentrated in counties with high crop specialization-where competitive vulnerability translates into concentrated losses. A commitment-politics framework organizes these patterns: railroads reduced the probability of being a market winner in high-TDE counties, where voters shifted from discretionary to commitment politicians. The 1890s episode is uniquely informative because, unlike today, there was fiscal and institutional room to rebuild trust: mainstream parties credibly adopted Populist demands, and the movement dissolved. Today those conditions do not hold-which may explain why modern populism has proven more persistent. * We thank the MUR-Prin grant PERCOP and the IGIER and Baffi research centers for financial support.

detail.title: Behind the ATM: Exploring the Structure of Bank Holding Companies

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Many modern banking organizations are highly complex. A “bank” is often a larger structure made up of distinct entities, each subject to different regulatory, supervisory, and reporting requirements. For researchers and policymakers, understanding how these institutions are structured and how they have evolved over time is essential. In this post, we illustrate what a modern financial holding company looks like in practice, document how banks’ organizational structures have changed over time, and explain why these details matter for conducting accurate analyses of the financial system.

title: The Costs of CSRD and CS3D to the European Union
affiliations: Brooklyn Law School

detail.title: The Costs of CSRD and CS3D to the European Union

declarations.funderStatement: Partially underwritten by Baron Public Affairs.

detail.abstract: This report examines the economic costs of the European Union's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D). Drawing on independent cost analyses and EU industry revenue data, the report finds that one-time compliance costs to bring EU supply chains into conformity with these directives range from €724 billion to €1.4 trillion, more than 300 times the EU Commission's own estimate. Annual recurring costs are estimated at up to €15.7 billion for CSRD and €10.2 billion for CS3D, with implicit conduct-change costs potentially reaching hundreds of billions more. Although reducing the number of directly covered firms, the December 2025 amendments largely leave the core climate transition and due diligence obligations intact. Beyond measurable costs, the report identifies substantial qualitative harms. These include higher consumer prices, novel and uninsurable civil liability exposure, and a fundamental transfer of corporate governance authority to broadly defined "stakeholders." * President, Furchtgott-Roth Economic Enterprises. This report was partially underwritten by a grant from Baron Public Affairs, a firm that advises several American companies adversely affected by CSRD, CS3D, and related European regulatory efforts. The report has benefited from constructive comments from outside referees. The conclusions, and any mistakes, in this report are entirely those of the author and should not attributed to anyone else.

title: Information Regulation as Antidiscrimination
affiliations: George Washington University Law School

detail.title: Information Regulation as Antidiscrimination
detail.abstract:
Employment discrimination law is under sustained retrenchment, nowhere more so than in hiring, the gateway to work and the foundation of equal employment opportunity. A recent executive order declared the disparate impact theory—a key doctrine of hiring equality—unconstitutional and barred its use by the federal government. The Supreme Court’s curtailment of race-conscious admissions has cast serious doubt on the future of affirmative action in employment. Enforcement agencies have redirected their efforts, abandoning disparate impact suits, scrutinizing employers’ diversity initiatives, and soliciting claims by white men. These developments further weaken a regime that has long struggled to redress discrimination at the hiring stage. Nearly a quarter century after audit studies revealed that identical resumes yield markedly different outcomes depending on whether they bear Black- or white-sounding names, hiring discrimination against Black applicants and other underrepresented groups persists.

This Article advances a theory of information regulation as antidiscrimination to confront these challenges and to remedy enduring gaps in employment discrimination law.  Effective enforcement of Title VII presupposes that workers possess sufficient information to identify and contest discrimination. Yet rejected applicants typically lack meaningful insight into employer decisionmaking. At the same time, employers have broad access to information about applicants—even trivial cues such as names—that can trigger significant bias. Recognizing that job applicants are outsiders to the firm, the Article conceptualizes hiring discrimination as a double-sided information problem: too much potentially biasing information flows to employers, and too little enforcement-relevant information flows to candidates. If discrimination in hiring is structured by information flows, it can be mitigated by recalibrating them. 

The Article develops a set of interventions designed to restructure the informational architecture of hiring. Ignorance measures—such as anonymized resumes, skills-based screening, and targeted “don’t ask” rules—limit employers’ access to information that facilitates discrimination. Transparency measures—such as disclosure of hiring criteria or reasons for rejection—equip applicants with the knowledge needed to vindicate statutory rights.  In proposing reforms, the Article draws on emerging bipartisan initiatives to articulate a politically durable template for information regulation as antidiscrimination that can be justified in the language of both equality and merit.  In an era of civil rights contraction, reorienting employment discrimination law around information regulation provides a stable foundation for workplace equality.

title: Growth of Stablecoin Cards in Southeast Asia: Infrastructure, Economics, and Regulatory Implications
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Growth of Stablecoin Cards in Southeast Asia: Infrastructure, Economics, and Regulatory Implications
detail.abstract: Stablecoin-linked payment cards have emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments of the digital payments ecosystem, with global monthly transaction volumes rising from approximately $100 million in early 2023 to over $1.5 billion by late 2025, a compound annual growth rate of roughly 106 percent. This paper examines their development in Southeast Asia, a region that has become a critical laboratory for stablecoin-based retail payment infrastructure. Focusing on Singapore-based StraitsX and its partnerships with Visa, RedotPay, KBank (Thailand), and Grab, the analysis integrates global growth metrics, Singapore's regulatory trajectory from Project Orchid through Project BLOOM, and the fee economics of stablecoin cards for merchants and consumers. The paper contrasts Singapore's proactive, sandbox-driven regulatory clarity with more enforcementoriented or restrictive approaches in Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. It further situates Southeast Asia within the global stablecoin landscape, contrasting the MAS model with the U.S. GENIUS Act (signed July 18, 2025). Drawing on blockchain analytics, official regulatory disclosures, and industry data, the paper argues that Southeast Asia's experience offers key lessons for policymakers, merchants, and consumers regarding the future of digital retail payments. The paper concludes with implications for regulatory design, consumer protection, and the competitive dynamics between incumbent card networks and new blockchain-native entrants.

title: Beyond Intergovernmental Relations in Federal Systems: The Concept of Intergovernmental Law

detail.title: Beyond Intergovernmental Relations in Federal Systems: The Concept of Intergovernmental Law
detail.abstract:
In federal systems, irrespective of the official division of powers, the development and implementation of public policy increasingly require the input of various orders of government. Concerted action is an everyday phenomenon in wide ranges of domains, such as health care, immigration, transportation, environmental protection, public safety, and pandemic management.

Countless studies have explored intergovernmental interaction in federal systems, both from a political science and policy perspective. Faced with federal realpolitk, law is often considered to be “beside the point.” While constitutional law provides a backdrop (particularly the division of powers, courts and second chambers), law is otherwise largely a blind spot of federal studies. And yet, in democracies founded on the rule of law, all public action must, at some point, be grounded in law. This is also true of federal democracies. The production and implementation of law in complex intergovernmental contexts are oddly understudied, as are the processes of accountability for intergovernmental executive action.

To shed light on the various ways through which legal norms, principles, processes and institutions shape federal governance, this paper introduces the concept of Intergovernmental Law (IGL). I posit that IGL has three main components. Upstream, it is composed of constitutional norms and institutions that shape intergovernmental action. Downstream, IGL includes processes of judicial review and parliamentary scrutiny of administrative and executive action taken in an intergovernmental context. And, midstream, it comprises specific toolboxes of legislative and executive law-making devices that help structure interactions and create complex normative networks.

Cheryl Saunders’ scholarship in domestic and comparative constitutional law informs almost every aspect of the overarching concept of intergovernmental law. This article is a tribute to Cheryl’s invaluable contribution to federal studies, notably her efforts in shedding light on the role of law in shaping federal theory and practice.

title: Betting on the State: Sports Gambling Legalization and Municipal Borrowing Costs
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Betting on the State: Sports Gambling Legalization and Municipal Borrowing Costs
detail.abstract: I estimate the effect of online sports betting legalization on U.S. state government borrowing costs in the municipal bond market. Using a stacked difference-indifferences design with secondary market bond-month observations, I find that legalization reduces bond yield spreads by 6 to 10 basis points. This effect is robust across three alternative spread measures, holds when using either never-treated or not-yet-treated states as the control group, and emerges gradually over the quarters following legalization. Mechanism evidence suggests a positive net fiscal effect: legalization increases state tax revenue, including about an average of $53 million in annual dedicated sports betting tax collections for the treated state, while state expenditure on health, police, welfare, and hospitals does not change significantly.

title: Submission on the Commission Proposal for the Digital Omnibus (Digital Package on Simplification)
affiliations: OsloMet - Oslo Metropolitan University and

detail.title: Submission on the Commission Proposal for the Digital Omnibus (Digital Package on Simplification)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Feedback on the proposed GDPR amendments in the Digital Omnibus proposal from Emily M. Weitzenböck & Samson Y. Esayas, in our capacity as independent researchers.

contentType.other: Comment submitted to the European Commission

contentFormat.other: Comment following the European Commission's call for feedback on the Digital Omnibus (Digital Package on Simplification)

detail.abstract:
We welcome the Commission’s efforts to simplify and optimise what has become an intricate web of digital rules spread across various EU legislation and appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback. While the proposed changes in the Digital Omnibus are comprehensive, this submission focuses on selected aspects of the amendments to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR). The proposed Digital Omnibus (DO) suggests various substantive changes to the GDPR in Article 3 DO. We consider the proposed changes concerning the introduction of EU-wide lists of processing activities requiring DPIAs and the development of common templates, as well as the amendments relating to breach notification obligations to be positive and consistent with the stated rationale of the Omnibus initiative, namely simplification. However, the DO also contains amendments that appear more substantive in nature. These elements have particularly attracted our attention and form the basis of the comments provided in this submission.

 Our feedback is limited to proposed amendments on the following:

-            the notion of personal data: proposed amendment to Article 4(1) and Article 41a GDPR

-            personal data processing and AI: proposed Article 9(2)(k), Article 9(5) and Article 88c GDPR

-            data subject’s right to access: proposed amendment to Article 12(5) GDPR

-            automated individual decision-making: proposed amendment to Article 22 GDPR

We limit our submission to the Commission’s adopted text and do not comment on any other subsequent drafts or texts by other EU institutions or bodies.

title: Applying the Central Clearing Mandate: Different Options for Different Markets
affiliations: Kiffmeister Consulting, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal and Financial Law Unit

detail.title: Applying the Central Clearing Mandate: Different Options for Different Markets
detail.abstract: Back in 2009, G-20 leaders have called for all standardized over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives to be cleared through central counterparties (CCPs). By now, 18 of the 24 Financial Stability Board (FSB) member jurisdictions have provided for mandatory central clearing frameworks in place, covering at least 90 percent of all standardized OTC derivatives in their jurisdictions. However, the authorities in several countries remain confronted with the hows and wherefores of mandatory central clearing, also in light of the international dimension of OTC derivatives contracts. This paper examines the policy options available to countries that have yet to fully conform to the clearing mandate, centered on the setup of local CCPs or on the use of foreign CCPs, and elaborates on their feasibility, risks and benefits from an economic, legal and tax viewpoint.

title: Does a Firm's Political Orientation Influence its Global Sales Diversification?
affiliations: University of Texas at San Antonio

detail.title: Does a Firm's Political Orientation Influence its Global Sales Diversification?
detail.abstract: This study examines how the political leanings of a firm's decision-makers influence its global sales diversification among US public companies. Drawing from the social cognition literature, we argue that liberal-leaning environments foster openness, adaptability, and a propensity to embrace diverse markets. We hypothesize that firms with a stronger liberal orientation among their leadership teams, boards, and headquarters locations are more likely to expand globally and achieve greater success in global markets. Empirical tests using a sample of about 30,000 firm-year observations of U.S. firms confirm this hypothesis. Our findings reveal that firms with more liberal political environments are more likely to expand globally and exhibit higher global sales ratios. The relationship remains robust after addressing endogeneity concerns through firm fixed effects, exogenous CEO turnovers, and instrumental variables. Furthermore, the effect of the political environment on global sales ratios is more pronounced for firms offering differentiated products and facing higher import competition. Liberal-leaning firms are also more likely to expand beyond their home region, particularly to Asia-Pacific. Higher global sales ratios are associated with increased firm value, especially for liberal-leaning companies. These findings suggest that liberal orientations are associated with unique intangible capabilities conducive to succeeding in global markets.

title: Reporting under Imperfect Information
affiliations: , University of Maryland, College Park and University of Maryland, College Park

detail.title: Reporting under Imperfect Information
detail.abstract: We experimentally study how uncertainty about the true state shapes reporting behavior when payoffs increase in the reported outcomes. In a chip-draw experiment, subjects report the number on a randomly drawn chip. In one treatment they observe the number directly, while in the other they observe only a signal that restricts the set of possible values without identifying the true number. We find that imperfect information substantially reshapes the distribution of reports: when the true state is uncertain, the majority of subjects report the highest value consistent with their signal. At the same time, imperfect information does not increase the frequency of incomemaximizing reports. These results indicate that imperfect information can systematically change the distribution of reported outcomes through a mechanism that differs from direct misreporting of a known state.

title: Technology Solutions to Support Central Bank Digital Currency with Limited Connectivity A Review of Existing Approaches
affiliations: Kiffmeister Consulting and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Technology Solutions to Support Central Bank Digital Currency with Limited Connectivity A Review of Existing Approaches
detail.abstract: This note explores the implementation of central bank digital currencies in environments with limited connectivity, emphasizing the need for offline solutions to enhance financial inclusion. It discusses various scenarios, such as stored-value card systems and device-to-device payment methods, which allow transactions without constant internet access. Key considerations include the form factor of devices, operational risks, and privacy issues associated with offline transactions. The note highlights the importance of security measures, diverse technological solutions, and user experience in the design of these systems. It explains that no single architecture fits all use cases, underscoring the need for continuous stakeholder engagement and adaptation to evolving technologies. Ultimately, the report advocates for robust offline payment systems that can effectively meet the challenges of limited connectivity while fostering resilience and inclusivity in financial systems.

title: A Network Approach to Scope 3 Emissions
affiliations: Vlerick Business School, Students, KU Leuven - Faculty of Business and Economics (FEB), Candriam Asset Management and Vlerick Business School

detail.title: A Network Approach to Scope 3 Emissions
detail.abstract:
We develop a network-based methodology to estimate firms’ indirect greenhouse gas emissions across upstream and downstream value chain tiers. The model initially requires monetary transaction data and suppliers’ and clients’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions, 
but we show that comparable results are obtained using only the existence of transactional links, without requiring monetary values.
Applying the method to global supply chain data from FactSet combined with Trucost emissions data, we find that our approach yields higher upstream emissions estimates for roughly 60% of firms between 2010 and 2021. Additionally, we find that downstream emissions account for the majority of indirect emissions, averaging about 61% of total value chain emissions. 
We validate the model by exploiting a subsample of firms with SBTi-verified Scope~3 targets as a proxy for higher-quality reporting. Across multiple matched samples, SBTi-certified firms exhibit significantly lower absolute discrepancies between reported and estimated emissions, suggesting that data quality is a primary driver of estimation error rather than systematic bias in our methodology.

reference: Journal of Engineering Research, volume 14, issue 1, 2026[10.1016/j.jer.2025.10.003]
title: Exploring the Mediating Role of Green Logistics in Enhancing Green Supply Chain Performance: Evidence From Bangladesh
affiliations: American International University-Bangladesh and Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP) - Centre for Higher Studies and Research

detail.title: Exploring the Mediating Role of Green Logistics in Enhancing Green Supply Chain Performance: Evidence From Bangladesh

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Engineering Research, volume 14, issue 1, 2026[10.1016/j.jer.2025.10.003]

detail.abstract: This study aims to investigate the mediating role of green logistics in enhancing green supply chain performance in the context of Bangladesh, focusing on the relationships among green procurement, eco-friendly transportation, sustainable manufacturing, and reverse logistics. A quantitative research methodology was employed, utilizing a structured questionnaire distributed to 425 professionals in various industries. A total of 276 valid responses were analyzed using Smart PLS to assess the relationships and mediating effects of green logistics. The findings indicate that green procurement and sustainable manufacturing significantly enhance green supply chain performance. In contrast, eco-friendly transportation and reverse logistics do not exhibit direct effects; however, their impact is mediated by green logistics. The study reveals that green logistics serves as a crucial enabler for integrating sustainability practices within supply chains. The results provide valuable insights for businesses and policymakers in Bangladesh, highlighting the importance of investing in green logistics strategies to improve operational efficiency and sustainability outcomes. By fostering sustainable supply chain practices, organizations can contribute to environmental preservation and social responsibility in the Bangladeshi context. This research fills a critical gap in the literature by examining the mediating role of green logistics in a developing country, offering a comprehensive framework that integrates multiple sustainability dimensions. The study is limited by its focus on a single country and the use of convenience sampling, which may impact the generalizability of the findings.

reference: International Review of Economics & Finance, volume 107, 2026[10.1016/j.iref.2026.105140]
title: In Gold and Franc We Trust? Rethinking Safe Havens in Europe
affiliations: , National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens - Faculty of Economics and Rzeszow University

detail.title: In Gold and Franc We Trust? Rethinking Safe Havens in Europe

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Review of Economics & Finance, volume 107, 2026[10.1016/j.iref.2026.105140]

detail.abstract: Given the critical need for portfolio diversification, we analyze the interdependencies of gold and the Swiss Franc with European stock markets. Using the R 2 decomposed connectedness approach and an extensive dataset spanning May 1, 2004, to May 31, 2025, we investigate the dynamic interactions separately within developed and emerging markets. Our findings reveal that total connectedness is stronger within developed markets and prone to several extraneous disruptions. While the Swiss Franc imports shocks from developed markets but acts as a volatility exporter in emerging markets, gold consistently demonstrates shock-absorbing behavior in both domains. We further assess their effectiveness in risk mitigation by using bivariate and multivariate portfolio strategies. The Swiss Franc offers considerable hedging advantages for developed stock portfolios, especially during financial turmoil, though these attributes wane in emerging markets. In contrast, gold is not an effective hedging tool in neither market type. The multivariate hedging strategy generates suboptimal risk reduction in emerging economies compared to developed ones and, under specific conditions, proves futile. Furthermore, bivariate portfolio analysis shows that gold provides superior risk-adjusted returns in both settings and under all market regimes. Although the Swiss Franc's inclusion often reduces Sharpe ratios, it emerges as a more defensive asset for downside protection during crises. Notably, the multivariate portfolio methodology is crucial for attaining higher Sharpe ratios in emerging markets, even though it doesn't improve risk-adjusted performance in developed markets. These findings become essential for investors and policymakers managing the complexities of modern financial markets.

title: The (Ir)Rationality of Firms' Forecasts
affiliations: Economic Statistics Centre of Excellence - ESCoE, University of Augsburg - Department of Economics, Athens University of Economics and Business and University of Augsburg

detail.title: The (Ir)Rationality of Firms' Forecasts
detail.abstract: Using a novel data set of continuous forecast errors in firms' own sales growth, we document that only major forecast errors-those in the two tails of the distribution-are predictable and autocorrelated. This pattern is robust and constitutes a sharp violation of the Full-Information Rational Expectations (FIRE) hypothesis. In contrast, minor forecast errors, while often economically meaningful, exhibit neither predictability nor autocorrelation. We show that these new empirical facts are consistent with a rational inattention framework in which firms optimally choose how much costly information to process. When information-processing costs are high, firms devote limited attention, leading to large forecast errors that are predictable and negatively autocorrelated. Our model also accounts for why predictability and autocorrelation collapse for small errors and matches additional features of the data, such as the negative autocorrelation in sales growth.

title: Assessing Nonlinear Price Risk and Systemic Contagion in Renewable Dominated Electricity Markets under Compound Extreme Weather Shocks
affiliations: North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and North China Electric Power University

detail.title: Assessing Nonlinear Price Risk and Systemic Contagion in Renewable Dominated Electricity Markets under Compound Extreme Weather Shocks

keywords.keywords: Risk diffusion；Compound climate shock； Systemic price risk； Stochastic market modeling； Market volatility diagnostics

detail.abstract: Accelerating market integration of renewables has significantly increased the exposure of electricity spot markets to weather-induced volatility. However, the complex nonlinear coupling between multi-source meteorological factors and grid constraints often leads to systemic price contagions that traditional risk assessment models fail to capture. This paper develops a source-grid-load coordination framework to evaluate systemic price risks and trace contagion pathways under compound extreme weather shocks. We first construct a weather-aware electricity trading model that integrates a day-ahead market clearing mechanism with coupled scenarios of wind speed, solar irradiance, and temperature. To capture the complex risk dynamics, we employ the Conditional Value at Risk method to quantify nonlinear price spillovers and identify systemic contagion among market nodes. The framework is applied to a regional power grid in northern China with high renewable penetration to validate its effectiveness in revealing risk transmission pathways and quantifying systemic spillovers. Results indicate that systemic price risk under compound climate scenarios is stratified and nonlinear and static compound scenarios pose the highest risk. Temperature-driven demand crossing system flexibility thresholds and nonlinear interactions between wind and solar generation are identified as the primary mechanisms amplifying systemic risk.

title: Effects of Trade Barriers on Foreign Direct Investment: Evidence from Chinese Solar Panels
affiliations: Comillas Pontifical University

detail.title: Effects of Trade Barriers on Foreign Direct Investment: Evidence from Chinese Solar Panels
detail.abstract: The return of protectionism and industrial policy will affect the international allocation of resources beyond the short run. To understand these long-term effects, I study the anti-dumping and countervailing Duties (AD-CVD) implemented by the Obama Administration in 2012 on Chinese solar panel imports. Due to their differential exposure to US trade policy, Chinese firms are granted different AD-CVD rates. I leverage this variation to develop a difference-in-differences design. I estimate the effect on Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) decisions by Chinese firms using a Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood method and data on FDI announcements from 2009 to 2015. My findings show that in 2012, targeted firms increase FDI by 145 million dollars per year from a previous average of 9 million dollars. These results are more economically relevant and last longer when considering only intensive-margin effects. However, the main findings for greenfield investment do not carry over to cross-border mergers and acquisitions. I use location choice models to test different hypotheses for FDI location. I find evidence of production fragmentation in Asia after the duties, mostly to countries that become exporters of solar panels to the US. These results document FDI diversion that modifies investment patterns in the short run and eludes the trade barriers in the medium run, weakening the intended effects of the protectionist policy.

title: Non-Labor Income Shocks and Women's Physical Activity Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design
affiliations: Wuhan Sports University

detail.title: Non-Labor Income Shocks and Women's Physical Activity Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of a critical leap in non-labor income on women's physical activity. Using data from the China General Social Survey (CGSS) (N=13464), disentangle the tension between the 'resource effect' and the 'status effect'. Findings reveal that crossing the 30% non-labor income threshold significantly increases women's physical activity, supporting the resource effect. However, this leap simultaneously reduces women's labor income share, weakening their household bargaining power and generating a negative status effect that partially offsets these benefits. We conclude that while non-labor income relaxes budget constraints, preserving women's economic bargaining power is critical for sustaining long-term health investments.

title: Energy poverty and climate change: a vulnerability framework for a tropical context
affiliations: Universidad EAFIT - School of Economics and Finance - Center for Research in Economic & Finance (CIEF), University of Manizales, Universidad EAFIT and Universidad EAFIT

detail.title: Energy poverty and climate change: a vulnerability framework for a tropical context
detail.abstract: Global warming is increasing households’ exposure to extreme thermal conditions, particularly in tropical regions. This study conceptualizes energy poverty as the inability to maintain safe thermal conditions under climate change, conditional on housing quality. Focusing on Colombia, we combine estimated thermal exposure derived from an adaptive comfort model and discomfort degree-hours with a municipal index of housing informality, adapting the Poverty Adaptive Degree-Hour Index (PADHI). The results reveal pronounced territorial heterogeneity. While some regions are primarily affected by thermal stress, others are dominated by structural housing deficits, and several territories exhibit the coexistence of both factors. These patterns highlight that energy poverty in tropical contexts cannot be explained solely by income or access to energy services. The study proposes a replicable framework for tropical countries and underscores the need for integrated policies that jointly address climate adaptation and housing improvement.

title: Climate Fairness and Growth: Allocating the Remaining Carbon Budget
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz, University of Luxembourg, Universite du Luxembourg and

detail.title: Climate Fairness and Growth: Allocating the Remaining Carbon Budget
detail.abstract: Limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees requires that cumulative carbon dioxide emissions remain within a finite remaining carbon budget. How this budget is allocated across countries raises questions of fairness and development. This paper evaluates whether equity-based carbon allocations are compatible with sustained economic growth in emerging and developing economies. We compute country-level fair shares of the remaining carbon budget under the equal-cumulative-per-capita (ECPC) principle. Using data for 162 countries between 1950 and 2023, we then estimate the historical relationship between income and per-capita CO2 emissions across income groups and use these elasticities to simulate cumulative emissions until 2050. Our results show that ECPC implies strongly negative remaining carbon budgets for most advanced economies, while lower-income countries retain positive but constrained allocations. Under historically observed income-emissions elasticities, many developing countries would exceed their fair shares when converging toward advanced-economy income levels. At the aggregate level, unused allocations offset only about 17% of the combined carbon budget shortfall implied by countries exceeding their allocation and the negative fair shares arising from historical responsibilities. In a scenario in which we assume that the technology of advanced economies is transferred to all countries, which would lower emission intensities, we find that some countries such as India, Egypt or Indonesia would now be able to economically develop within their fair budgets. At the aggregate level, however, technology transfer would only increase the carbon budget coverage to approximately 38% and would not fully eliminate the gap.

title: Corporate Communication in Practice
affiliations: Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies-Technical Campus

detail.title: Corporate Communication in Practice
detail.abstract: This chapter examines the practical applications of corporate communication within organizations, focusing on four critical areas: developing strategic communication frameworks, understanding organizational communication flows, conducting corporate identity audits, and implementing corporate advertising initiatives. The material integrates theoretical frameworks with real-world case studies from Indian and global organizations to provide comprehensive understanding of corporate communication practice.

title: The Humane Management of Adolescents’ Challenging Behaviour in Out-of-Home Care: A Cross-sectional Study of Staff Evaluations
affiliations: Oulu University of Applied Sciences, University of Helsinki, University of Eastern Finland and University of Eastern Finland

detail.title: The Humane Management of Adolescents’ Challenging Behaviour in Out-of-Home Care: A Cross-sectional Study of Staff Evaluations
detail.abstract:
There is a growing global need for out-of-home care (OoHC) placements for children and adolescents, who represent one of the most vulnerable groups in Western societies. Challenging behaviour is common among individuals in OoHC, who are exposed to restrictive practices that may compromise their wellbeing.

This study aimed to describe staff competence in the humane management of challenging behaviour in OoHC services in Finland. The research addressed three questions: (1) How frequently do Finnish health and social care professionals in OoHC encounter challenging behaviour, and what kinds of associations does it have with their well-being? (2) How do Finnish health and social care professionals in OoHC evaluate their humane and comprehensive management of challenging behaviour? (3) How is the behaviour management training received during formal education or the continuing training received at work associated with perceived competence?

A cross-sectional study was conducted and reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology checklist. Data were collected with the Humane and Comprehensive Management of Challenging Behaviour instrument during February–March 2024, with 170 frontline professionals participating.

Challenging behaviour was frequent, with nearly 70% of staff encountering it daily or weekly. Behaviour management training improved staff competence in supporting children’s and adolescents’ self-regulation skills.

Challenging behaviour places psychological strain on OoHC staff, but targeted training can strengthen professionals’ capacity to support self-regulation, which is essential for adolescents’ positive development and long-term outcomes. The findings support developing multidisciplinary child welfare units with strong mental health expertise providing humane, safe care.

title: Energy Efficiency and CO₂ Emissions in Eco-Innovative Brazilian Sectors: A CGE Sensitivity Analysis
affiliations: Federal University of Juiz de Fora, Federal University of Juiz de Fora, Federal University of Juiz de Fora and Federal University of Juiz de Fora

detail.title: Energy Efficiency and CO₂ Emissions in Eco-Innovative Brazilian Sectors: A CGE Sensitivity Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the sensitivity of Brazil's key eco-innovative sectors (Extractive Industry, Manufacturing Industry, Transportation, Energy, and Gas) to reductions in the use of fossil inputs in their production processes. Although eco-innovation is increasingly recognized as a crucial driver of energy efficiency and emissions mitigation, evidence on its sector-specific macroeconomic and environmental effects in emerging economies remains limited. Against this backdrop, this paper assesses how productivity gains in these sectors can enhance energy efficiency, reduce pollutant emissions, and influence household welfare and overall economic performance. Using a Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model with an emissions module and a Social Accounting Matrix (SAM), the analysis evaluates the long-run impacts of productivity shocks across eco-innovative activities. The findings indicate that such shocks would increase GDP, household consumption, and the trade balance over time. The Manufacturing Industry stands out with the most significant economic gains, but it would also experience an increase in CO₂ emissions. In contrast, the Extractive Industry, Transportation, and Energy sectors would show reductions in emissions. These results highlight the complex interactions between productivity improvements, economic growth, and environmental sustainability, offering relevant insights for the design of sector-specific policies aimed at reconciling competitiveness with Brazil’s low-carbon transition.

title: Deep Research on a Loop: Using AI Agents to Construct Economic Datasets
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Buenos Aires (UBA) - Faculty of Economic Science, Students,  and University of San Andres (UdeSA)

detail.title: Deep Research on a Loop: Using AI Agents to Construct Economic Datasets
detail.abstract: Constructing datasets from primary sources is among the most costly stages of empirical research. We propose Deep Research on a Loop (DRIL), a methodology that uses AI agents to assemble datasets from publicly available sources. DRIL applies a research agent iteratively across a defined unit space (e.g., countries by years), guided by a formal research instrument that specifies variables and coding rules, an evidence policy governing source hierarchies and citation standards, and data quality mechanisms that track gaps and uncertainty throughout. A two-stage architecture separates research design from research implementation. We outline a replication-based evaluation framework that compares DRIL's output to published datasets constructed by human researchers. Empirical results are forthcoming. We argue that even partial automation of dataset construction can shift the production function of empirical research.

title: Successfully Fired: The Unique Incentives of Agentic-AI Adoption *
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Texas at Dallas - School of Management - Department of Finance & Managerial Economics

detail.title: Successfully Fired: The Unique Incentives of Agentic-AI Adoption *
detail.abstract: We study optimal incentive contracts when workers privately observe whether Agentic AI can automate their jobs. Firms balance bonuses for truthful reports of successful automation with termination threats. Workers may be fired regardless of automation success (mass termination), even though dismissing non-automatable workers destroys value. Mass termination becomes more likely when automation probability rises or workers capture more surplus. Firm value is convex in automation probability, while worker utility is non-monotonic, rationalizing divergent attitudes toward Agentic AI. Mass layoffs increase in frequency over time without improvements in automation, and are less likely in firms employing many similar workers.

title: Rolling Difference-in-Differences Estimation for Small and Large Panels
affiliations: and Michigan State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Rolling Difference-in-Differences Estimation for Small and Large Panels
detail.abstract: We introduce lwdid, a Stata command that implements the rolling differencein-differences (DiD) estimator proposed by Lee and Wooldridge (2025). The rolling approach transforms the panel-data DiD problem into a sequence of cross-sectional treatment-effect estimation problems, allowing flexible estimation of treatment effects in settings with staggered adoption and treatment-effect heterogeneity. The command is further designed to accommodate both large and small panels. In particular, it also implements the extension developed in Lee and Wooldridge (2026) for small-panel settings, where the number of cross-sectional units is limited and conventional large-sample asymptotic inference may be unreliable. For large panels, a key feature of lwdid is that it provides computationally efficient inference using a multiplier bootstrap based on exact influence functions of the estimators. Because this approach avoids repeated model estimation, it substantially reduces computational cost. For settings with a small number of units, lwdid also provides valid inference procedures. Under normality, exact inference can be conducted using t-distribution, while HC3-based inference and randomization inference (RI) are provided as alternatives that require weaker assumptions. Overall, lwdid provides applied researchers with a practical and efficient tool for estimating treatment effects within the rolling difference-indifferences framework.

title: Stablecoins in the USA: Politics, Markets, and Rules
affiliations: Emory University and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Stablecoins in the USA: Politics, Markets, and Rules
detail.abstract: We examine how stablecoins moved from the periphery of cryptocurrencies and regulatory scrutiny to becoming a centerpiece of strongly bipartisan-supported U.S. legislation. We argue this happened because stablecoins came to be seen as a source of political power, particularly for actors with an interest in sustaining dollar dominance. To build support for this claim, we analyze the institutions, ideas, and interests that shaped the GENIUS Act. First, we highlight how the President's Working Group reframed stablecoins as a prudential and payments problem compatible with existing institutional arrangements. Second, we trace the ideas that shaped the legislation, including stablecoins as a private-money problem, a payments innovation, an instrument of dollar statecraft, and a politically viable alternative to central-bank digital currencies (CBDCs). While these ideas were not always harmonious, together they pushed policy toward allowing regulated, privately issued payment stablecoins. Third, we examine how interest groups reshaped both the debate and framing around legislation. We conclude by assessing the GENIUS Act's achievements and examining the questions it leaves unanswered.

title: On Simulation Pseudo-Bias and Truncation in the Modified Harmonic Mean Estimator
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics

detail.title: On Simulation Pseudo-Bias and Truncation in the Modified Harmonic Mean Estimator
detail.abstract: The modified harmonic mean estimator developed by Gelfand and Dey (1994) for the marginal likelihood exhibits a smaller computational bias—known as simulation pseudo-bias—than the original estimator proposed by Newton and Raftery (1994). Simulation pseudo-bias occurs in importance sampling when the simulated samples from the proposal distribution have narrower empirical support than the target distribution, even if their theoretical supports are identical. The modified estimator mitigates this pseudo-bias by changing the importance sampling target from the prior density to a weighting density parameterized by posterior samples. Furthermore, the pseudo-bias correction method provides a computational rationale for the truncation embedded in commonly used weighting densities. Empirically, this paper revisits the finding of Smets and Wouters (2007) that the marginal likelihood of their DSGE model is comparable to that of a VAR model. Using various harmonic-mean-type estimators, I confirm the robustness of their original finding, which was based on the local Laplace approximation. I also demonstrate that relying on pseudo-biased estimators leads to an erroneous preference for the DSGE model.

detail.abstract: This paper provides empirical verification and a practical applied framework for the Helioeconomic Theory of Long-Wave Cycles (Valkov 2025, 2026a), which proposes that Kondratiev waves equal the sum of five solar cycles (T(K) = Σ5•SC ≈ 55 years) with troughs at SC_peak+3 minima. Verification proceeds at three levels. First, a six-indicator cross-cycle comparison between the K5 descending phase (1969-1996) and K6 onset (2024-) confirms directional alignment across gold, inflation, interest rates, equity valuation, commodities, and geopolitical conflict clustering. Second, statistical analysis of the NBER recession database (n=34, 1857-2020) shows 38% of recessions onset within ±12 months of solar cycle maxima versus 20% expected (χ²=8.7, p=0.003). Third, the Gnevyshev gap is verified as a leading indicator across five historical solar cycles (SC16-SC23, lead time 1-3 months) and confirmed in real time: the SC25 gap of-166 EISN units (February 24, 2026) preceded the US/Israel strikes on Iran by four days-the shortest lead time in the series. Two concurrent real-time conflict outcomes (Russia-Ukraine: COW failure confirmed March 2026; Iran-USA/Israel: preliminary failure ongoing) provide additional verification of the war-cycle mechanism developed in companion paper Valkov (2026b). Applied sections derive a full investment phase calendar (2024-2072) across seven K/SC transitions, an asset class positioning matrix with K5-analogue returns (gold price corrected to ~$5,117 (March 9, 2026; ATH $5,600 January 28, 2026)), and a corporate strategic planning matrix across nine sectors. Seven explicit falsification criteria are formalised; two are confirmed as of March 2026 (Gnevyshev gap → Iran crisis; Russia-Ukraine failure).

detail.abstract: This paper develops the Helioeconomic Theory of Long-Wave Cycles, proposing that Kondratiev waves equal the sum of five consecutive solar cycles: T(K) = Σ5•SC ≈ 55 years. This formula provides the first physically grounded mechanism for long-wave periodicity. A companion trough rule establishes that Kwave troughs coincide with the solar minimum of the third cycle following the K-peak (SC_peak+3), verified with month-level precision for K4 (February 1944, Δ<1 month) and K5 (August 1996, Δ<5 months) against SIDC v2.0 data. A three-level model is developed: Level 1-the K-wave (~55 yr) defines epoch character; Level 2-the solar cycle (~11 yr) times crises within each wave; Level 3intra-cycle structure (Gnevyshev gap, last-surge pattern) provides 4-day to 3-month leading indicators. Statistical analysis of the NBER recession database (n=34, 1857-2020) shows 38% of recession onsets within ±12 months of solar maxima versus 20% expected (χ²=8.7, p=0.003). The Gnevyshev gap is verified as a crisis leading indicator across five solar cycles (SC16-SC23, lead time 1-3 months). A sixth real-time instance is documented: SC25 EISN drop of-166 units on February 24, 2026, preceded the US/Israel strikes on Iran by four days-the shortest lead time in the series. Two concurrent real-time conflict outcomes (Russia-Ukraine: COW failure confirmed; Iran-USA/Israel: preliminary failure ongoing) provide independent verification of the war-cycle mechanism, developed in full in a companion paper (Valkov 2026b). War cycle analysis is not reproduced here; readers are referred to the companion paper. Current position (March 2026): K6 descending phase, SC25 post-maximum, with three independent real-time framework predictions simultaneously confirmed.

title: Low Fertility and Fiscal Sustainability: The Effects of Past and Future Fertility Rates on the US Federal Budget Outlook

detail.title: Low Fertility and Fiscal Sustainability: The Effects of Past and Future Fertility Rates on the US Federal Budget Outlook

publicationDetails.detailsText: Aspen Economic Strategy Group Policy Paper Series 4/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Aspen Economic Strategy Group Policy Paper Series

detail.abstract: Low fertility and population aging have shaped the U.S. federal government’s spending and revenue patterns, contributing in large part to the growing federal debt. This paper examines the role of these trends in shaping America’s current fiscal position and the potential for a reversal of these trends to relieve domestic fiscal pressures. The authors find that the dramatic rise in fertility rates during the Baby Boom has led to a marked rise in old-age entitlement spending, as this cohort entered retirement. Rising life expectancies have also been a significant driver of increased entitlement spending and will continue to place pressure on federal deficits and debt in the coming decades. This paper then evaluates how near-term fertility trends would affect the federal budget under a baseline scenario of continued low fertility and an alternative scenario in which the US returns to a replacement-level total fertility rate in 2026. Under both scenarios, deficits and debt are projected to remain on an unsustainable path through 2055, as changes in the fertility rate today would take multiple decades to meaningfully impact the size of the working-age population. In fact, the budget outlook is somewhat worse under the replacement fertility scenario, and demonstrably so if we factor in the costs of pronatalist policies that might be needed to achieve replacement fertility. In the outlook beyond 30 years, higher fertility would gradually improve the fiscal position. However, given the current unsustainable trajectory of the US federal debt, it is possible that changes in tax or spending policy would need to occur before the fiscal benefits of higher fertility rates could be realized.

title: Legal Protection of Free Speech and Corporate Innovation
affiliations: University of Groningen

detail.title: Legal Protection of Free Speech and Corporate Innovation
detail.abstract: I show that legal protections for free speech foster corporate innovation. Exploiting the staggered adoption of anti-SLAPP statutes across U.S. states, I find that stronger speech protections increase patent applications by 19%, with effects concentrated in breakthrough patents and new technology classes. I develop a model in which anti-SLAPP laws raise the reputational cost of incumbent technologies by enabling credible public scrutiny, inducing firms with lower switching costs to preemptively innovate. Effects are strongest among firms with high intangibility, R&D intensity, and environmental exposure, and absent for financially constrained firms. Industry-level innovation efficiency dispersion narrows, consistent with a technology-screening mechanism.
